## China's EV industry wasn't planned into existence — local credit bought the right of way

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-17-chinatalk-中国电动车不是北京规划出来的-是地方政府用信贷买路权买出来的/
- 节目 / show: ChinaTalk (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/chinatalk/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: The Rise of China’s Electric Vehicle Industry
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-17 · 时长 / duration: 1:54:15
- 文稿来源 / transcript: YouTube captions · 17938 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**This episode takes half the credit for the rise of China's carmakers away from central industrial policy: the real engine was local governments trading loans and equity for factories, and entrepreneurs using relationships to route around SOE licensing — at the cost of an overcapacity nobody can now unwind.**

为什么听 / why: Essential if you want first-hand field research rather than another industrial-policy survey: Geely talking to 60 cities to fund the Volvo purchase, the chain of imitation after Hefei rescued NIO, BYD trading light rail lines for taxi orders — all of it raw detail.

### 核心论点 / points

[5:12] (樊明路) **One number — 150,000 units — decided which carmakers were allowed** — In the 1990s China sold only about 500,000 passenger cars a year, a market the size of Poland then or Vietnam today, yet every province except Tibet had its own car plant; a count in the mid-1990s found roughly 130 carmakers. The reason was not absurd: under a system of planned allocation, if you wanted cars you had to build them yourself. Volkswagen and other foreign partners told Chinese regulators that a car plant needs at least 150,000 units a year to be efficient, and so ‘150,000’ became the magic number in policy circles — with a market under 1 million units, it could hold only four to six companies. That simple piece of arithmetic produced the ‘three bigs and three smalls’ list of designated licensees directly.

[11:19] (樊明路) **Chery was never a private firm; it was one prefecture city's SOE** — Chery was not a state firm belonging to a big province, a big city, or the central government — it belonged to Wuhu, a city in Anhui. In the early 1990s Wuhu could not find a pillar industry, then discovered a township and village enterprise on the city's outskirts turning out three to five thousand cars a year using engineers from a Hunan arms plant and Korean KD kits, priced at roughly $10,000 (70,000-80,000 yuan), far below the joint-venture cars of the three bigs and three smalls; it became the first company in Wuhu to pass 100 million yuan in revenue. The city concluded from this that ‘carmaking can work’, first tried to partner with FAW and failed, then took the 200 million yuan from selling its Saiwen plant (later Conch) plus bank loans arranged by the province and bought an engine production line in Wales, in Britain — because the lesson FAW had taught them was that without your own engine you cannot build your own car.

[21:27] (樊明路) **The barrier then was not technology or capital but the license** — For its first few years Chery could not obtain a central production license, so it could sell only inside Anhui province, and one province's market cannot support a carmaker. Their solution was to sell cars in Chengdu while having buyers accept Anhui plates. The first party that could not tolerate this was not consumers but the Chengdu public security bureau, which notified buyers directly that they had to register locally. The detail shows where the barrier sat in those years: not in technology and not in capital, but in administrative permission itself — the cost of routing around a license was high enough to make people invent a transaction structure this ridiculous.

[35:34] (樊明路) **Geely did not pay for Volvo; local banks did** — Ford's condition was ‘if you can raise the money, we'll sell’, so Geely's core work through all of 2009 was assembling about $2 billion. An investment banker involved in the deal says Geely talked to as many as 60 cities — out of roughly 300 prefecture-level cities nationwide, one in five. The pitch was to show local officials Volvo's next-generation product line (the cars that later became the XC60 and XC90): I will let you build some of these models, and in exchange you put up ‘five fingers’ — 500 million yuan, then about $70-80 million, as the ticket to ride, in the form of credit from local banks or equity injected into an SPV. Line up four or five cities and the system turns. The biggest early backer was in fact Beijing, and there was even a letter from a Beijing municipal leader to Ford's CEO serving as an endorsement, but in late 2009 BAIC came out against the city supporting a competitor at home, and Beijing withdrew.

[41:44] (樊明路) **The NDRC handed out permission, not funding** — Geely did not force its way through: it waited until it had the NDRC's unwritten approval before it moved. In 2007-08 the earliest candidates to buy Volvo were state firms like Changan, and all of them ultimately said they did not have the money or that it was not a priority; only after the NDRC had confirmed that no SOE wanted to buy did it let Geely proceed. The contrasting case is another private Sichuan company that wanted to buy Hummer, announced the deal itself without approval, and left regulators in Beijing to learn about it from newspapers and television — the deal was strangled outright. After approval the center's attitude was: financially, you sort it out yourself. Policy banks including the Export-Import Bank refused to lend at first, and only once Geely had raised the entire amount was CDB willing to lend for the plants that came next.

[55:01] (樊明路) **BYD was selling local governments a megaproject, not cars** — The ‘10 city thousand vehicle’ program handed the targets to local governments, and BYD found the arbitrage inside it: localities had to deliver a record of achievement, BYD needed volume. In partner cities like Shenzhen and Changsha it converted entire taxi fleets to its own electric cars (in 2008-09 the Changsha government sold a bus plant to BYD outright), and it built its own finance company to help taxi drivers and bus operators buy the vehicles; Shenzhen had no Olympics and no World Expo, so it used the Universiade to run its own demonstration project, and BYD accounted for a quarter of the 2,011 vehicles in service. The more important chip was a dedicated rail transit division it set up — it could tell a local government: if you want more, I can build you a light rail line, so you can hand your superiors a ‘big project’. Through the 2010s it sold only about 30,000 cars a month, which earned it the nickname ‘30,000 units’; this state-business exchange is what kept it alive.

[1:04:06] (樊明路) **Hefei made three to four times its money; the imitators got only capacity** — NIO was at first extremely unwilling to take local government money, because it came attached to a mass of conditions (how much you must invest locally, and so on). Once its cash ran out and its US-listed shares collapsed at the end of 2019, it had no other option. Beijing again withdrew at the last moment because BAIC objected; Hefei took over, injecting about $1 billion (7 billion yuan) of equity, and exited completely on the stock market roughly a year later at three to four times its money. The problem came after that: the Hefei model was treated nationwide as a template, at exactly the moment the NDRC had already stopped approving new vehicle capacity in 2020-21. Guangdong province and Guangzhou injected about 2 billion yuan into XPeng, and Ningbo about 10 billion yuan into Geely's Zeekr, all of them counting on reproducing that ‘three-to-four-times exit’ — and after 2021, with Chinese listings abroad and EV valuations crushed together, the exit route was gone while the money had already been turned into capacity.

[1:12:13] (樊明路) **The Changan-Dongfeng merger has stalled a year on two host cities** — The other way to digest the surplus is SOE consolidation, but that road is harder than it looks. Since last year the center has gone beyond rumor to something more concrete, requiring the relatively successful Changan and Dongfeng to merge; nearly 12 months of pushing has produced no result, because Chongqing and Wuhan, the two home cities, will neither of them give ground, and it is now basically shelved. This stands in contrast to more than a decade of centrally driven SOE mergers that succeeded in other industries, and it explains why autos has never been an industry the center administers directly: in the 1980s China tried establishing a national company to run all of the country's car plants, and it survived only a few years before dissolving, because localities were unwilling to give up their own plants.

[1:28:33] (樊明路) **Exports are near twice Japan's peak, and that curve cannot hold** — Extrapolating from this year's pace, China's vehicle exports for the full year could reach about 12 million units. The reference point is Japan's export peak (around 1986) of roughly 6 to 7 million units, which set off the US-Japan and Europe-Japan trade wars — China is already close to twice that. So the guest argues the curve is unsustainable: you cannot imagine exports of 15 million next year. The EU is plugging the gaps, and a policy proposal extending high tariffs from pure EVs to plug-in hybrids has already appeared. The real way out is local production, and the opportunity sits precisely in European carmakers' own idle capacity: Europe's automakers have been hit both by Chinese cars (not only electric ones, combustion cars too) and by over-expanding after overestimating demand during the pandemic, and with young people buying fewer cars and even getting driver's licenses less often, what the European market faces may not be stagnation but decline.

### 术语 / glossary

## When a child asks permission for everything, the problem is perfectionism, not the child

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-17-parentmojo-孩子不需要你给出答案-只需要一个脚手架/
- 节目 / show: Your Parenting Mojo (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/parentmojo/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Re-release: Creative Problem-Solving (Without Giving the Answer)
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-17 · 时长 / duration: 54:08
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Official transcript · 8207 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- 校验 / verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A four-and-a-half-year-old boy comes home from preschool and starts asking permission for everything; his mother finds that when she sets perfectionism aside and stops handing him answers, his ability to solve problems on his own far exceeds what she expected.**

为什么听 / why: This is a real one-on-one parenting coaching conversation, not a research review; there is no new data, but the minimum viable move of not giving the answer, and the self-doubt of an immigrant mother, are both very concrete.

### 核心论点 / points

[6:02] (Sara) **"Be the best" is a lesson in "you are not good enough"** — Sara grew up in a family whose motto was "be the best." Her parents meant well, of course, but no one person can come first in academics, sports, music and art all at once, so from very early on "be the best" got bound up, in her mind and in her body, with "you are not good enough." She started experiencing anxiety at 9 or 10, and it got worse as she grew up. She knew she absolutely did not want the same thing for Som, so she and her husband agreed early on: no pushing him to perform, follow his interests instead. That starting point comes out of her own experience, not out of an abstract philosophy.

[7:58] (Sara) **The first thing preschool taught him was to ask permission first** — A year after Som started preschool, beyond separation anxiety, his behavior changed noticeably too: when he wanted to draw, he would come and ask, "Can I get the markers?" There is a yes space in Sara's home, and he had always simply taken materials off the shelf himself, so this asking put her on alert. Her guess is that it came back with him from the preschool environment, where anything you do has to go through an adult first. And the relationship she cares most about is this one: at home, "no" is for genuinely unsafe situations, and everything else was supposed to be a yes by default. That is what pushed her to look for tools to supply the missing learning support at home.

[11:04] (Sara) **An immigrant's self-doubt turns most easily into enrichment-class anxiety** — Her son had just turned four, and every child his age around him was signed up for swimming, soccer, ice skating, even musical theater. As an immigrant, Sara started doubting herself over and over: what if these extracurriculars are exactly what this society requires? What if not signing him up leaves him behind, and it is all my fault? On a coaching call in the membership course, Jen asked her, "Who is the child in front of you?" and then had her think about her own core values. Those two prompts became her compass every time she wavered, and they also stopped her from convicting herself on the grounds of being an outsider.

[14:56] (Sara) **Perfectionism comes back in through judgments about the learning itself** — Sara used to believe deeply that setting impossible standards for herself was what got her where she is, and that is in fact true, but the price was paid by her mind and body. In her behavior she could hold back from straightening the sticker Som had stuck on crooked, but she had not noticed that perfectionism had simply changed form: she kept judging their learning explorations together as "not creative enough, not deep enough." Once Jen named that as perfectionism, both her anxiety and her guilt eased. Now, when the critic starts up in her head, she says to herself: "That's perfectionism talking."

[22:00] (Sara) **There is only one first step: do not give the answer** — When she first joined the Learning Membership, Sara was quite lost about the very concept of "learning exploration" and did not know what her own position in it should be. The simplest entry point Jen gave her was this: start by not giving your child the answer, and the later steps will follow naturally. So she practiced saying "I wonder why," "What do you think?" and "Let's go to the library and find a book." A year later this has become second nature, and not only for questions of fact: when a real conflict comes up, she brainstorms with him too, and sometimes the solution comes from Som himself. That one minimum move takes the adult down from the position of knowing everything.

[29:25] (Sara) **Give the smallest possible step and the child extrapolates the rest** — Sara says she no longer worries about giving a wrong answer or about her child not being able to answer. The path a child learns by is to observe patterns, propose theories, then extrapolate from the experience he already has — an iterative process that keeps correcting itself, driven by inner curiosity. In the drone example, seagulls were being disturbed by a drone and Som asked "What is a drone?" She knew that this time she had to supply a bit of key information, so she explained that it flies by remote control. Som immediately thought of his own remote-control helicopter and talked for 15 minutes straight about roughly how drones fly. The adult gave only the smallest step, and it landed exactly on the knowledge he already had.

[35:19] (Sara) **A torn cheese lid counts as a real problem-solving workout** — On the way home from grocery shopping, Som was eating sliced cheese and tore off the resealable lid, which Sara had told him beforehand not to tear. She was very tired that day and a little irritated, and halfway through what she was saying she realized this was a problem-solving opportunity, so she asked: "What could we do so the cheese doesn't dry out?" Som said "I don't know" at first; she asked again, and he answered right away, "Put it in a Ziploc bag." Something that would have left them both feeling bad turned into a genuine bit of mental exercise. Sara says it took almost no effort, because a year of practice has already built the reflex.

[51:26] (Sara) **What matters most is not reading, writing and arithmetic, but metacognition** — Looking back at where she was a year ago, Sara says what she would tell her earlier self is: you don't actually know yet what matters most. A year ago she thought the most important things were reading, writing and arithmetic; now she genuinely believes the most important skills Som can learn are creative problem solving and metacognition. Supporting those does not require a lesson plan — only quiet observation, giving him time and space, respecting his interests, and then adding a little scaffolding from the side. If she had known this last year, she says, things would have been a lot easier. This is close to where the whole method in the episode finally lands.

### 原话 / verbatim quotes

[6:02] Sara: "I grew up in a family where the motto was be the best. And of course, I couldn't be the best at everything, academics, sports, music, art, so from a very early age, being the best was paired with you're not good enough in my brain and my body."
    译 / zh:

    译 / zh:

    译 / zh:

## The Troubles were not a religious war but demographic anxiety and zero-sum politics

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-16-restishistory-北爱冲突不是宗教战争-而是人口与经济的零和博弈/
- 节目 / show: The Rest Is History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/restishistory/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: 697. The Troubles: Murder in Belfast (Part 1)
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-16 · 时长 / duration: 1:26:16
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 15362 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**For decades Britain ignored the demographic anxiety and economic imbalance inside Northern Ireland and left the problem to the streets; in the summer of 1966, while Londoners cared only about the World Cup, the violence in Ulster was about to run out of control.**

为什么听 / why: If you assume the Troubles were religious hatred or a sudden eruption, this episode overturns that picture: the real triggers were Protestant demographic fear, the indifference of British politicians, and a flag.

### 核心论点 / points

[3:39] (Dominic) **The old anti-papal register was announcing a new anxiety about identity** — The episode opens with Ian Paisley's sermon of March 1, 1965, "Why I Am a Protestant." He prays that God will "utterly smash the chains of the sin of apostasy," and warns that the inheritance of Ulster's Protestants is being sold out. The problem is that at a moment when London was wearing miniskirts and NASA was preparing to land on the moon, this sixteenth-century anti-papal register was completely out of place. Paisley was a hardline fundamentalist, an opponent of the Roman Catholic Church all his life and a supporter of Ulster loyalism. He would later share power with the republican Martin McGuinness in a joint Northern Ireland government, the two of them nicknamed the Chuckle Brothers. But in 1965 his sermon was already an announcement: Northern Ireland held an anxiety about identity that refused to be swallowed by modernity.

[7:08] (Tom) **The dead were not politicians but shop assistants and schoolchildren** — Tom gives the numbers for the scale of the conflict: at the peak in the early 1970s, nearly 500 people were killed each year, and Belfast had a bomb almost every day. The list of victims is not politicians but shop assistants, barmen, singers, barbers, housewives, schoolchildren -- people who died simply because of which denomination their name sounded like it belonged to, which church they walked into, or which street they lived on. British MPs, and the Queen's cousin Lord Mountbatten, were also killed by bombs in 1979. These details pull the conflict back from abstract politics to specific people: this was indiscriminate violence between communities, and any ordinary person could become a target because of a marker of identity.

[9:17] (Tom) **Where you begin the history is itself a political position** — Tom points out that where you start telling the Irish story is a political choice. The British version tends to say the violence erupted out of nowhere, while Irish nationalists begin with the Norman invasion, Elizabeth I, Cromwell, the Plantation of Ulster. This episode picks up in the early twentieth century: the island then held about 4.5 million people, three quarters of them Catholic, with Protestants concentrated in six counties in the northeast. That demographic pattern alone determined the geography of the conflict to come. Each narrative selects its starting point in order to prove who has legitimacy -- so "where does the history begin" is not an academic question but a political position.

[22:09] (Dominic) **No Surrender was a cry of demographic anxiety, not of doctrine** — Dominic works through the deepest Protestant fear: Catholic families had more children, and the Catholic population would eventually outnumber the Protestant one. One line from Terence O'Neill, Northern Ireland's prime minister in the 1960s, caused public outrage: his reason for treating Catholics better was that "then they will have fewer children." That instrumental demographic calculation made Catholics angrier, and it turned Protestant defensiveness into political mobilization. Paisley's favorite slogan was "No Surrender," and it was precisely a product of demographic anxiety. The logic shows that the root of the conflict was not abstract doctrine but a zero-sum imagination created by a majority/minority structure.

[43:04] **MPs knew less about Northern Ireland than about distant colonies** — British politics long assumed the Irish question was settled -- Northern Ireland had its own parliament and its own devolved powers, and London had no need to get involved. Only when Labour backbenchers launched the Campaign for Democracy in Ulster did the press begin reporting the discrimination Catholics faced in housing and voting rights. But the episode quotes an MP of the time admitting that most MPs knew less about Northern Ireland than about colonies on the other side of the world. That systematic indifference meant tensions inside Northern Ireland kept accumulating with nobody sounding a warning, and it also explains why the violence that followed caught Britain off guard.

[51:17] **Foreign investment landed only in the east, making the growth plan an accelerant** — O'Neill came to power in 1963 and decided the first challenge was the economy. He brought in multinationals such as Michelin, Ford and ICI, hoping foreign capital would create jobs and modernize the place. But the investment concentrated in Belfast and the east, and unemployment in the Catholic districts of the west did not improve. Worse, the work discipline of the new industries clashed with local habits of life, and the foreign-owned factories were seen as an invasion by an outside culture. In practice O'Neill's growth plan favored Protestants and the east, and so turned economic inequality into political grievance. The case makes the point: economic reform, if it is unbalanced, is an accelerant of conflict.

[1:05:41] **A flag there is not a symbol but a claim to sovereignty** — In the 1964 West Belfast election the republican candidate Liam McMillen hung an Irish tricolour in his window, and Paisley immediately organized a protest and demanded the police intervene. On September 28 the Royal Ulster Constabulary removed the flag by force, setting off the worst rioting since the 1930s. A flag is only a symbol, but on the community boundaries of Northern Ireland it is a claim to sovereignty. The police chose a side, which left the Catholic community feeling that the machinery of the state was not a neutral arbiter. The episode treats this as an important starting point for the Troubles; it shows that in a society this sensitive, any visible symbol can set the streets alight.

[1:22:47] (Tom) **The summer England won the World Cup, the UVF had already begun** — Tom reminds listeners that the summer of 1966 was the moment of Swinging London and England's World Cup win, and mainstream Britain was paying no attention at all to Northern Ireland. To them it was just "people shooting at each other in a faraway place," nothing to do with Carnaby Street and miniskirts. But it was in exactly that summer that the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) began to act, and O'Neill had to hurry back to Stormont from a holiday in France. London's cultural carnival and the shadow of violence over Belfast form a jarring contrast, and that mismatch was both an attitude of indifference and the reason Britain's political elite had almost no early-warning mechanism before the crisis escalated.

## TSMC Trucks Half-Finished Wafers Between Fabs: The Secret Weapon of AI Capacity

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-16-asianometry-台积电用货车把旧厂改造成-ai-新产能/
- 节目 / show: Asianometry (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/asianometry/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: How TSMC Uses Old Fabs to Make New Chips
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-16 · 时长 / duration: 15:47
- 文稿来源 / transcript: YouTube captions · 2500 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**TSMC exploits the more than 90% tool overlap between N5 and N7 to truck half-processed wafers from its Tainan fab to Taichung for finishing, freeing up AI capacity while N5 converts to N3. The foundation of the AI boom is a fleet of ordinary trucks.**

为什么听 / why: This episode uses Mark Liu's and C.C. Wei's own words from earnings calls to puncture the stereotype that a node transition requires a new fab. The information density is high, and the second half, on trucking wafers between fabs, is especially counterintuitive.

### 核心论点 / points

[0:05] **The money spent this year only becomes capacity two years later** — TSMC is building new fabs in three places in Taiwan at once: Fab 20 in Baoshan, Hsinchu; Fab 22 in Nanzi, Kaohsiung; and Fab 25 in Taitung, which so far is only land. There is also AP7, an advanced packaging fab in Chiayi. More than $60 billion in capital expenditure has already been allocated for 2026. Yet C.C. Wei and other executives concede that the money spent in 2026 will not reach the market until 2028. AI demand still cannot be met, and Nvidia wants chips now. TSMC holds one more card: cross-node utilization.

[1:08] **Node names mean nothing; the real node is a set of tools** — The most open secret in semiconductor manufacturing is that logic node names mean nothing. TSMC's node roadmap is not a straight line from N3 to N2 to A14; it splits like ASCII art. N3 branches into N3E, N3P, N3X and N3C; N2 branches into N2P, N2X and A16. Once a node enters the fab, the manufacturing team keeps experimenting and yields climb point by point into the mid-80s. When enough improvements accumulate, they get repackaged as a new node -- N6 was born out of N7 -- or the improvements are saved for a future node. In the end, a node is a collection of tools and recipes.

[4:10] **The end of depreciation is not pure profit; old fabs get stranded** — One of a fab's biggest costs is depreciation, a non-cash charge that stands for the useful life of the tools. After five to seven years the fab is fully depreciated, and in theory everything left after operating costs is profit. In reality tools always break, which is why Charlie Munger called EBITDA "BS earnings". When a large customer moves up a node, the old fab is left with an enormous hole in its capacity: Apple moved from N7 to N5, and the Taichung fab had to go find another customer. N2 is too new and too strange, N3 is the sweet spot, N4 is mature and still leading, while N7 and N6 are stuck in the middle -- too far from the frontier, and expensive next to 28nm. Once utilization drops below 70%, a fab starts losing money.

[7:10] **Above the transistor, the layers can be identical across nodes** — A semiconductor is stacked in layers: transistors at the bottom, and above them the copper or aluminum metal interconnect layers, the BEOL. The finest lines are in the lowest metal layers -- N5's M1 has a pitch of roughly 28-30 nanometers -- and the higher you go the wider they get, up to 1.5 or even 3 microns at the top. That structure is shared across nodes, so many process steps are the same or similar between N16, N10, N7, N6, N5, N4 and N3. The critical transistor layers do differ, but the layers above the transistor can be completely identical. This is also why old DUV machines are still in heavy use. For the past decade, TSMC has used this layer overlap to keep its fabs from being stranded.

[9:15] **N10, N7 and N5 are really one single pool of capacity** — In 2015, co-CEO Mark Liu said on an earnings call that 20nm and 16nm had 95% tool overlap, so a customer that wanted to upgrade could have its 20nm capacity converted to 16nm. In 2018, C.C. Wei said N10, N7 and N7+ had 90% overlap -- N7+ being the custom version with EUV added, built for Huawei. CFO Laura Ho added that the overlap from N7 to N5 was also more than 90%. That means N10, N7 and N5 can be treated as one enormous pool of capacity, and old fabs need not sit idle when customers move up. Conversion is not free, but it saves billions of dollars of capital expenditure.

[10:15] **The claim that N7 could not convert to N3 expired within a year** — The AI era needs a great deal of N3 capacity. N5 and N3 have 90% tool overlap and both sit in Fab 18 in Tainan, connected by a giant wafer bridge, so conversion is easy. In 2024 TSMC began converting N5 to N3, at the cost of a bite out of gross margin. On the Q1 2024 earnings call, C.C. Wei was asked whether N7 could be converted to N3 in the same way. He said it was much harder, because N5 and N3 are in the same fab while N7 is in Taichung, about 100 miles away; he also said N7 demand would come back. By early 2025 he had changed his answer: for future AI products (that is, Vera Rubin) converting N5 was necessary, but N5 demand was strong as well, so the timing had to be chosen carefully -- and they had already worked out a way for N7 capacity to support N5.

[13:17] **The foundation of the AI ecosystem is a fleet of low-tech trucks** — Once TSMC's wafers leave the front-end fabs, they have to travel to the advanced packaging fabs in Chiayi or Miaoli for CoWoS and InFO. How do you move wafers worth $20,000 each? In semi-custom modified trucks, carrying a few dozen FOUPs, running on Taiwan's highways like any ordinary freight vehicle. TSMC's ESG site even discusses improving working conditions for the truck drivers. Now TSMC is scaling that trucking service up massively: the Tainan fab processes only the critical N3 or N5 layers, then the unfinished wafers are loaded onto trucks and driven 100 miles to Taichung, where the underutilized N7/N6 fab finishes them. That lets Tainan put everything into the critical work. The largest infrastructure on earth, the foundation of the AI ecosystem, rests on a fleet of low-tech trucks.

### 术语 / glossary

- cross-node utilization (): Treating the capacity of several logic nodes as one unified pool, meeting new demand by converting old fabs and shipping wafers between them.

- CoWoS (): TSMC's 2.5D advanced packaging, which places multiple dies on a silicon interposer and interconnects them.
- FOUP (): The standard wafer carrier, protecting wafers inside the fab and in transit. The transcript renders it as FOOP.

[41:51] (Jolene Ramsey) **The phage has to act early, because once σA binds it cannot be evicted** — GP27 is the key protein that forms the condensate: its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) binds DNA, while its folded region interacts with the beta subunit of RNA polymerase. GP33 is an inhibitor of the host sigma factor σA; it binds between σA and the beta subunit and blocks the transcription complex from entering a productive transcription state. [1:19:55] **Smallpox gene loss is a continuing process that had already begun in medieval times** — In the CAM208 genome, 49 genes are deleted or inactivated. [1:40:45] (Rich) **The marginal notes in Jenner's own book are today's anti-vaccine talking points** — Rich shares a scan he found of an original copy of Jenner's An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, and discovered that the book once belonged to the Southampton Anti-Vaccination League: its pages carry a large number of handwritten annotations by anti-vaccinationists. [1:52:54] (Brianne) **Reading is not an instinct, and AI makes judgment scarcer still** — Brianne shares The Atlantic's article ‘The End of Reading’, which notes that in 2022 fewer than half of adults had read any book at all. ## The Roman Empire ran on enslaved people, not on its legions

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-16-ancients-罗马帝国是奴隶制的产物-无奴隶则无帝国/
- 节目 / show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: How Slavery Built the Roman Empire
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-16 · 时长 / duration: 1:07:26
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 11181 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Rome's administration, its army, its domestic work, its workshops and its mines ran almost entirely on enslaved people; after Carthage fell in 146 BC slavery became the engine of the economy, and once Augustus stopped expanding, that population reproduced itself by birth.**

为什么听 / why: Dense with information, and it explains the mechanism through specific people and specific laws rather than generalities. It corrects the impression that ‘slavery was just one facet of Rome’. Worth hearing all the way through.

### 核心论点 / points

[2:27] (Emma Southern) **Take slavery out of Rome and the whole stool falls over** — Emma answers the title head-on: the Roman Empire simply could not have existed without slavery. From the bureaucracy to paying the army, almost everyone who handled the paperwork was enslaved or freed; hauling stone, building roads and keeping cities running all depended on enslaved labour. Her image for it: pulling slavery out of Rome as a whole is like pulling one leg off a three-legged stool — the whole thing cannot stand. She then stresses that the experience of enslaved people was deliberately fragmented. People at different ranks under the same roof competed with each other rather than combining, and that was an order the rulers maintained on purpose.

[8:25] (Emma Southern) **A freedman's freedom could be taken back at any time** — Rome wrote slavery into law very early. The Twelve Tables already contain clauses on the sale of people and on manumission. The freed were called freedmen: legally neither free persons nor slaves, but a stratum wedged between the two, barred from holding public office, unable to enter into certain contracts, with the restrictions reaching their children as well. Crueller still, being ‘insufficiently grateful’ could be grounds for re-enslavement. Emma stresses that this design was not an accident but an extension of Rome's bureaucratic character: a human being is a special kind of property, but property all the same.

[13:03] (Emma Southern) **Saying ‘slave’ finishes the Romans' work of turning people into things** — Emma argues that the word ‘slave’ is itself an instrument of dehumanisation, converting a person into an abstraction. She advocates ‘enslaved person’, which forces the speaker to pause for half a second and remember that the other party was a living human being. Her example is the gravestone of a three-year-old boy who died in an aristocratic household, paid for by his parents, who describe themselves as husband and wife — something legally impossible for them. From the stone you can work backwards to the mother's pregnancy, her work, her labour and delivery, even though none of it was ever written down. Archaeological material gives you fragments only; the rest has to be completed by imagination.

[19:59] (Emma Southern) **Only after Carthage was destroyed did Rome become a slave economy** — Emma dates the change in the character of Roman slavery to the fall of Carthage. Before it, Rome won and lost against the Samnites and the Etruscans in turn, citizens on the losing side could themselves be enslaved, and people flowed back and forth between wars. Once Carthage was destroyed, Rome swept the Mediterranean with no rival left and the number of war captives exploded; a few great estates were worked by whole blocks of enslaved labour, and Rome formally became a ‘slave economy’ — one that could not have held up for two hundred years without enslaved labour. Empire is extraction at bottom: alongside gold and silver, people were a resource being extracted.

[26:37] (Emma Southern) **Breeding kept the slave economy going for another 800 years** — After Augustus proclaimed the Pax Romana and closed the Temple of Janus, Rome stopped waging large-scale wars of expansion, and the supply of captive slaves fell sharply. But the slavery Rome practised was hereditary: a child born to an enslaved woman was born a slave. By then the enslaved population was already large enough to sustain itself by reproduction. Emma also points to an explicit incentive: an enslaved woman who bore three sons could obtain her freedom; daughters did not count. This self-reproduction extended the slave economy by roughly another 800 years.

[33:18] (Emma Southern) **The worst position of all was being enslaved with no master** — Not all enslaved people were foreigners. A Roman citizen could be sentenced to become a gladiator or sent to the mines or the quarries, which counted as a form of the death penalty. Emma calls them servus poenae, slaves of punishment: they had no particular owner, so there was nobody who could grant them favour and never any possibility of improving their situation. Beyond that, only two categories of enslaved people were protected in law: first, the stewards and outward-facing representatives of prominent families or the emperor's household; second, the publicly owned civic slaves of a city, for whom the city guaranteed housing, food and a small wage.

[1:00:16] (Emma Southern) **Buying your way to freedom was a road open only to men** — Emma points out that older scholarship overstated how common manumission was: the claim that ‘every slave was freed before thirty’ comes mainly from the experience of male bureaucrats and household slaves. In practice there were four routes: a gift from the owner, release by will, release after promotion through service, and saving up to buy yourself. Augustus restricted release by will: the individuals had to be named, and there was a ceiling on the proportion freed. But buying freedom was open almost exclusively to men. Emma says she cannot think of a single example of a woman purchasing her own freedom; an enslaved woman was usually freed by marrying her former owner, and in the same move was locked into a marriage that was very hard to leave.

[1:05:54] (Emma Southern) **A ‘good master’'s favour could be withdrawn at the last moment** — Emma closes with the case of Pedanius, a senator under Nero who was murdered by an enslaved member of his own household. By law every enslaved person in his house was to be put to death as collective punishment, and on that occasion 400 people were crucified. One motive Tacitus records is that Pedanius had first agreed to let his killer buy his freedom, then went back on it at the last moment. Emma uses this to show how fragile the Roman moral imagination of the ‘good master’ really was: favour at the very top could be revoked at any time, and the price of resistance for enslaved people was dozens or hundreds of lives.

### 术语 / glossary

- Pax Romana (): The long period of stability opened by Augustus, in which wars of expansion declined and the source of slaves shifted from war captives to birth within the household.

## America Rescued the Yen for Its Own Trillion in Treasuries, Not for Japan

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-15-patrickboyle-美国救日元不是为日本-是为自家万亿美债/
- 节目 / show: Patrick Boyle (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/patrickboyle/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: The Hidden Risk in the US-Japan Yen Rescue
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-15 · 时长 / duration: 31:36
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 4686 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The first US intervention in the yen in 28 years was officially a favor to an ally. The real calculation was to stop Japan from selling $1 trillion of US Treasuries to defend its currency — which would push up America's own cost of borrowing.**

为什么听 / why: One episode explains three things that make no sense on their face: why America intervened in the yen, why it sold euros to do it, and why Bessent is afraid of Japan selling Treasuries. You come away understanding what the disappearance of the Treasury convenience yield means.

### 核心论点 / points

[0:00] (Patrick Boyle) **The Treasury Secretary's sticky note broke a 28-year taboo** — The episode opens on an absurd detail: a sticky note carried by US Treasury Secretary Bessent into a cabinet meeting, reading "buy yen, $5-10 billion," with the currency code JPY thoughtfully appended. Trump later explained it aboard Air Force One as doing a friend a favor, and even brought up Pearl Harbor. The genuinely strange thing is not the note but the nature of the act: the last time the US Treasury stepped in to support the yen was 1998, 28 years ago. By convention a Treasury Secretary does not do this, which makes it worth asking what actually happened.

[4:14] (Patrick Boyle) **Carry trade profits are not free money but a fee for holding the grenade** — There is no mystery to the mechanics of yen weakness. The Fed raised rates to roughly 3.75% to fight inflation, while the Bank of Japan held at zero for years and only recently moved to 1%. That enormous gap created the global carry trade: borrow yen in Tokyo at almost no cost, swap into dollars, and buy Treasuries paying around 4%. The textbooks say this should not produce a free lunch — the low-yielding currency ought to appreciate by exactly enough to cancel the rate differential. For years the market has done the opposite, and economics calls the gap the forward premium puzzle. The more popular explanation is that what you earn is not free money but a commission for holding the grenade on everyone's behalf. When it blows up, everybody runs for the exit on the same day, and the yen appreciates violently.

[9:25] (Patrick Boyle) **America bailed out the currency of a country on its own watchlist** — The US Treasury's official position has not changed in decades: it does not intervene in exchange rates, it lets the market set value, and intervention is only a short-term band-aid. To police everyone else, it publishes a report every six months naming trading partners that manipulate their currencies. The latest report, in July of this year, listed 10 countries, and Japan was on it. Yet in that very same month the US Treasury went into the market itself to help Japan bid the yen up. Strictly speaking, what the report criticizes is holding a currency down to push exports, and this time the intervention pushed the yen up. But spending American taxpayers' money to move a currency you are actively monitoring makes it plain that the rules are there to constrain other people.

[12:31] (Patrick Boyle) **Washington funded the yen rescue by quietly selling euros, not dollars** — The execution is stranger still. When the New York Fed placed the orders with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley on the Treasury's behalf, what it sold was not dollars but euros — and the European Central Bank was kept in the dark. The bulk of the euro assets in the US Exchange Stabilization Fund are French government bonds, so there is a strong chance America was in effect dumping a batch of French sovereign debt. A senior ECB official described this to the FT as "an unprecedented breach of central bank etiquette," and the IMF handbook explicitly advises central banks not to intervene in other countries' currencies. It amounts to driving off in your neighbor's car without asking, hitting a tree, and then explaining to him why his premium is going up.

[14:43] (Patrick Boyle) **The rescue was aimed at Japan's trillion in Treasuries, not at the yen** — Friendship with Tokyo is not the point; America's own borrowing costs are. Japan is the largest foreign holder of US government debt, with more than $1 trillion. If Japan spends another $50 billion or $80 billion defending the yen, the most convenient way to raise the money is to sell Treasuries — and heavy selling would push Treasury prices down and yields up. That is exactly what Bessent most fears, which is why he wants to help Japan steady the yen. His résumé makes it more ironic: in 1992 he was at the Soros fund and watched the Bank of England get picked off, and he later made his name shorting the yen. Now, sitting in the US Treasury Secretary's chair, the thing he is defending against is precisely the playbook he ran 30 years ago.

[18:56] (Patrick Boyle) **A Treasury Secretary should not place directional bets through debt issuance** — For most of the past two years Bessent has tilted issuance toward short-term bills and been unwilling to issue long bonds. The stated reason is that long-end rates are high right now, so there is no need to lock in for 30 years. Underneath it is a directional bet — a wager that inflation comes down, long rates fall, and the debt can then be swapped into long bonds. That bet is fine coming from a hedge fund, but not from a Treasury Secretary, whose job is not to guess rates but to fund the government regularly and predictably. Unfortunately rates have not fallen: the 10-year has risen to roughly 4.6%, and the 30-year has broken 5%. As long as rates do not come down, his funding strategy is stuck in a loop of rolling short-dated paper at ever higher cost.

[25:09] (Patrick Boyle) **$88 billion bought two weeks, and half the gain was given back** — The intervention did work at first: at the end of July the US and Japanese authorities spent roughly $88 billion over two days, and the yen went from around 164 to 155, a move of about 5%. Within two weeks it had slid back to 159, giving up half of that gain. The reason is plain — the FX market trades trillions of dollars a day, and $88 billion is small change. Obstfeld calls this set of contradictory policies cakeism: America wants a weak dollar but no inflation, low borrowing costs alongside enormous deficits, and Japan to keep buying Treasuries while the yen strengthens. America's own tariffs and its pressure on Japan to invest in the US are themselves pushing the yen down. It is bailing water out of the boat while drilling holes in the hull.

[27:21] (Patrick Boyle) **Treasuries are no longer scarce, and that is the real foundation here** — The real foundation of this drama is not the yen but the scarcity of US Treasuries. A paper by Harvard professor Wenxin Du finds that the convenience yield the world pays for the safety and liquidity of Treasuries has been narrowing for decades and has recently vanished, even turning negative. The cause is supply: too many Treasuries have been issued, and they are no longer scarce. Thursday's 30-year auction cleared at 5.22%, already the highest 30-year borrowing cost for the US since 2001. If the goal is a stronger yen, the cleanest route is for the Bank of Japan to raise rates. But Japanese government debt is already above 200% of GDP, debt service eats a quarter of government spending, and the new prime minister is opposed to hikes. Intervention does not change the trend; at most it buys a few days.

## The Order Calls Vaccines Soda and Splits MMR Into More Shots: Every Sentence Is a Lie

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-15-twiv-行政令里的谎言-拆mmr与汽水比喻都是伪科学/
- 节目 / show: This Week in Virology (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/twiv/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: TWiV 1348: Clinical update with Dr. Daniel Griffin
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-15 · 时长 / duration: 55:00
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 9063 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Every sentence in the ‘gold standard’ executive order gets called a lie: splitting MMR to add needles, vaccines as bottled soda, Merck refusing outright — and the new CDC director will have to pick a side.**

为什么听 / why: High information density but no major scientific breakthrough; worth it for the policy fight, the outbreak numbers, and two mechanisms that are easy to overlook — mAbs interfering with vaccine response, and the wastewater score having no units.

### 核心论点 / points

[2:03] **The order is not a scientific assessment — every sentence in it is a lie** — The August 10 executive order asserts that ‘pure nations sustain high vaccination rates through public trust and education, while American states instead use mandatory school-entry requirements’. The conversation immediately dismantles that frame: this is not a scientific assessment, ‘every sentence in it is a lie’, and ‘gold standard’ is nothing more than a label. There is a real counterexample from the COVID period — some countries invested in education and had people scrambling to get vaccinated. But the 50 US states differ enormously, and trust and education alone cannot hold vaccination rates up.

[9:15] **Splitting MMR has no scientific rationale — it just means two more needles** — The order ‘acknowledges’ that measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis and polio, among others, should be recommended for all children — and then demands that MMR be broken into three single-disease shots, each given at a separate visit where possible. The key judgment: this adds needles and office visits, with no scientific reason at all, and no manufacturer is willing to make them. The reason Trump gave when signing was that combination vaccines contain a ‘dangerous amount of fluid’, describing a single shot as being like a bottle of soda; in fact most vaccines are only about 0.5 milliliters. Merck's answer was 10 years and hundreds of millions of dollars — and an explicit no.

[14:30] **Vaccination has always been a state power, so the order is an overreach** — Vaccination decisions in the US have historically belonged to the individual states; the federal role is to issue ACIP recommendations that the CDC director signs off on, which makes the executive order an overreach. This is the third executive order aimed at vaccines in under a year; the previous one was already blocked by a judge, and this one will most likely go the same way. The new CDC director previously said ‘they would never ask us to put children at risk’; now the order is sitting in front of her, and how she answers becomes the first test. HHS is also soliciting members for the National Vaccine Advisory Committee, and someone joked that being selected would mean the clinical updates have to stop.

[21:45] **The Cyclospora season has not closed out, and the risk sits in one production line** — CDC has received 13,895 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, with at least another 10,455 awaiting further investigation; Michigan alone accounts for 12,485 cases and 279 hospitalizations, and there have already been deaths. Missouri has 1,577 cases, New York City 594. August should be near the tail end of the imported season, some sources have been pinned down and the products pulled from shelves. The remaining risk is that 40% of US lettuce comes from Taylor Farms, and contamination on the Mexican production line is the main worry.

[23:51] **Screwworm kills not through the maggots but through secondary sepsis** — The US now has 45 screwworm cases, concentrated in New Mexico and West Texas. Mexico reported 204 cases between April 2022 and March 2026, of which 202 were analyzable: 72% male, mean age 61, 55% on the lower limbs, 77% with at least one comorbidity, six deaths, and only one attributed directly to the myiasis. The larval stage is an obligate parasite: eggs hatch in 12-24 hours, and the larvae feed on living tissue for 5-7 days before dropping to the ground. The mechanism of death is that in people with neuropathy the wound is eaten open, bacteria enter the bloodstream, and sepsis follows.

[28:58] **The county RFK once went to lobby has become the measles epicenter** — Measles has already reached 2,484 cases this year, with 10%-20% hospitalized, and there have been deaths. The New York Times dug up RFK telling the Amish community in Lancaster, Pennsylvania five years ago that the CDC and agencies like it ‘cannot stand that you are healthy’, and joking that the treatment for measles is chicken soup plus vitamin A. That same county is now one of the largest outbreak sites in the country, with the state reporting 230+ cases and physicians reckoning it is badly undercounted. The attitude here is unambiguous: hundreds of children hospitalized and unable to catch their breath is not something to discuss lightly.

[40:22] **Get a monoclonal first and the later vaccine's B cell response is suppressed** — A study in JID asked whether people who received a COVID monoclonal antibody during acute illness have an altered immune response to a subsequent mRNA vaccine. An analysis of 43 people showed that at day 140 neutralizing antibody titers were lower in the mAb recipients than in the placebo group, and RBD-specific memory B cells were reduced at both day 56 and day 140 — but spike-specific CD4/CD8 T cells were unaffected. The conclusion is that anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonals limit the RBD-directed B cell response to a later vaccine while leaving T cells intact. The unanswered question Griffin cares about is whether waiting three months or six months before vaccinating avoids the suppression.

[53:59] **The 2 on the wastewater chart has no units and is not a concentration** — A listener asked what the ‘2’ on the CDC wastewater chart actually is. The answer lays out the whole pipeline: sampling → concentration → nucleic acid extraction → qPCR or dPCR to get a concentration such as gene copies per liter → normalization for rainfall and sewage composition → conversion by service population into gene copies per person per day → and finally a 7- or 15-day rolling average with a regression fit. But Vincent stresses that the ‘2’ itself has no units; it is only a categorical score. Read on its own the number will be misinterpreted — it has to be looked at alongside hospitalization and emergency department trends.

### 术语 / glossary

- MMR / measles-mumps-rubella vaccine (): The routine three-in-one childhood vaccine; the executive order wants it broken into three separate shots.
- ACIP / Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (): A committee under the CDC that sets US vaccine recommendations, which then go to the CDC director for approval.
- lyophilized (): Drying a vaccine down to a powder, so it needs no cold chain and stays stable at higher temperatures.
- PICO / the PICO question framework (): The evidence-based medicine structure for a search question: population, intervention, comparison, outcome.
- sterile insect technique (): Releasing sterile males so that females, which mate only once, produce no offspring, suppressing the target insect population.
- RIG / rabies immune globulin (): Supplies passive neutralizing antibody for the roughly 7 days before the vaccine takes effect, used in post-exposure prophylaxis.

## The cure for picky-eating anxiety: no judgment, no rewards, dessert is just another food

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-14-raisinggh-挑食焦虑的解药-不评判-不奖励-甜点也是普通食物/
- 节目 / show: Raising Good Humans (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/raisinggh/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Picky Eating & Food Guilt with Jennifer Anderson
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-14 · 时长 / duration: 46:02
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 8503 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**A child's relationship with food does not hinge on whether they ate any particular thing. It hinges on whether the parent sorts food into good and bad, whether dessert gets used as a reward, and whether the parent gives themselves permission to feed according to what the child actually needs. The earlier picky-eating signals are recognized, the easier they are to change.**

为什么听 / why: For parents whose feeds are saturated with "good food, bad food" and who are simultaneously locked in battles at the dinner table with their kids and their own parents. Information density is moderate; the picky-eating warning signs and the scripts for hard conversations are the biggest additions.

### 核心论点 / points

[3:07] (Jennifer Anderson) **Loving your body and caring for your body are one thing, not two** — Jennifer uses her own coined phrase, "embodied independence," to make the point: a child needs to live inside their body and love it, and also be able to answer rationally what that body needs — bathing, a balanced diet. She insists these were never two separate things but a single one. Once the culture splits enjoying your body and caring for your body into two goals, the child ends up divided between "what I like to eat" and "what I should eat." Putting the two words side by side is precisely an attempt to pull that connection back together.

[6:57] (Jennifer Anderson) **Unless there is an allergy, every food can fit in a child's diet** — She argues social media's biggest distortion is sorting individual foods into good and bad. Those labels make parents anxious and guilty, and they transfer easily to the child. Her replacement is a flexibility frame: absent a diagnosed allergy or other medical reason, all foods can fit into my child's diet. The parent hosts the experiment — observing firsthand what works for their own family. The shift does not abandon health goals, but it takes fear and shame off the table, and parents become more confident as a result.

[13:49] (Jennifer Anderson) **Dessert should go directly onto the dinner plate** — Against the rule of "finish your meal, then you get dessert," Jennifer offers two alternatives. First, do not announce dessert before the meal, so the cookie is decoupled from dinner. Second, put a small portion of dessert right on the dinner plate and serve it as an ordinary food. She acknowledges the second is a culture shock for many families and may not suit them, but it has worked in her house. The key move is that the parent acts as the restaurant's chef: what goes on the table is your call, rather than something you direct verbally, nonstop, at the child.

[14:57] (Jennifer Anderson) **Balance is not taught by lecturing but by how often a food appears** — She rejects defining food through lectures and argues for teaching through frequency on the table: hyper-palatable foods are only "extra delicious," so they appear rarely; plain, high-fiber, high-protein foods appear often. Without hearing a single word, the child learns balance from the family table. She also warns against using food as a reward — "eat your spinach and you get a cookie" carries the subtext that the cookie ranks above the spinach, children grasp that instantly, so it is best not to make that trade at all.

[19:09] (Jennifer Anderson) **What decides the outcome is not which strategy you pick but how you say it** — The core is "not which strategy, but how you use it." The same sentence — "you can only have one piece of cake" — lands completely differently said with fear and moral judgment than said matter-of-factly. Jennifer suggests parents first work out whether they need a stricter or a looser environment, then give themselves permission to choose whichever fits their own relationship with food. A strategy that does not match the household's atmosphere cannot be sustained, however correct it is.

[23:52] (Jennifer Anderson) **The red flags for picky eating were visible at 10 months old** — Her son showed red flags at 10 months: he avoided purees and needed 20 exposures before he would eat a given food, at an age when children are usually very open. She did not wait for a doctor to say "let's keep watching" — she used the extreme-picky-eating screener (PSAE) as early as possible. Her son turned out to be an ordinary picky eater and never became an extreme one. Her rule of thumb for parents: a full year with no improvement, and still picky at 6, puts you in red-flag territory that needs to be taken seriously.

[31:09] (Jennifer Anderson) **Toddlers eating less is usually fine; rescuing the meal is the problem** — A toddler's falling appetite is not necessarily a problem: growth slows sharply after age 1, so eating less is a normal physiological change. But the moment parents panic and pull out chicken nuggets, snacks and other hyper-palatable foods to "rescue" the meal, the child loses interest in plain food instead. What really warrants attention is a sudden shift in eating around age 6 — starting to ask about sugar content, abruptly eating very little, or a 7-year-old coming home from school saying "I'm too fat." These are not parental failures; they are the signal to find a professional.

[39:12] (Jennifer Anderson) **"Don't tell your mom" is the line with grandparents that cannot be conceded** — When conflict with grandparents over snacks arises, Jennifer's approach is: first, expect to feel bad, and accept feeling bad; second, communicate through the channel the grandparents are used to, and offer concrete, cheap alternatives (buy a balloon, go to the zoo, rather than ice cream every time); third, when necessary, sit with the discomfort and set a hard boundary — she once told a relative that giving her child candy was fine, but "do not say don't tell your mom," and that was non-negotiable. She adds a further warning: comments about a child's body made to their face can affect them for life, and if the other person will not change, a short-term separation is safer than continuing to expose the child.

## El Niño Isn't a Short-Term Shock, It's a Permanent Loss of Growth

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-14-oddlots-厄尔尼诺不是短期冲击-而是永久性增长损失/
- 节目 / show: Odd Lots (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/oddlots/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: A Historic El Niño Is Coming That Could Cost the World Trillions
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-14 · 时长 / duration: 55:53
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Official transcript · 9045 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**El Niño is not just a passing weather shock: research shows it permanently depresses the path of economic growth, a single strong event can cost trillions of dollars within five years, and we have not adapted to it.**

为什么听 / why: El Niño is usually treated as a short-term disturbance, but this episode shows its long-run economic impact runs far beyond what that framing allows, with direct implications for how you think about climate risk and investment decisions.

### 核心论点 / points

[5:09] (Justin Mankin) **El Niño isn't the world getting hotter, it's the heat moving** — El Niño is an ocean-atmosphere interaction in the tropical Pacific, one half of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Normally the trade winds blow from east to west, piling warm surface water up in the western Pacific and forming a warm pool. When those winds weaken, the warm water spreads eastward and redistributes the energy that drives weather worldwide. Think of the difference between a room with a single space heater in one corner (La Niña or neutral conditions) and a room where an entire wall is a radiator (El Niño): the total heat the atmosphere is exposed to is a completely different thing.

[12:22] (Justin Mankin) **This one may be the strongest since 1950** — Every forecast model points to the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, and possibly stronger than the historic events of 1877-78 and 1882-83, 1997-98, and 2015-16. The Australian Bureau of Meteorology's Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) forecast reaches 3.3, which is unprecedented. Conditions are already at El Niño alert status, and every single forecast shows this event running warmer than the 2016 one.

[15:30] (Justin Mankin) **Peruvian potato farmers were forecasting El Niño five hundred years ago** — The modern scientific understanding of El Niño dates to the twentieth century, but archaeological evidence shows that Peruvian potato farmers five hundred years ago could already forecast it from the visibility of the Pleiades. El Niño changes the distribution of high cloud over the eastern Pacific, which affects how clearly the Pleiades can be seen, and farmers adjusted their planting dates accordingly. It is a demonstration of the value of folk meteorological knowledge, and it also means humanity's history of adapting to El Niño is in fact a long one.

[22:39] (Justin Mankin) **The peak is still ahead and the South Asian monsoon is already late** — El Niño typically peaks between December and February, but the effects have already begun. Since alert conditions were reached in June, the South Asian monsoon has been delayed, directly affecting food security for billions of people. A late monsoon forces farmers to irrigate, which pushes up diesel demand and from there feeds into prices and politics. There is a non-trivial probability that 2026 becomes the hottest year on record, and 2027 is all but locked in for record heat.

[31:46] (Justin Mankin) **The five-year loss is $5.7 trillion, not $36 billion** — A 2023 paper in Science shows that El Niño is not a simple level effect, where output takes a hit and then recovers. It systematically depresses the rate of growth, so the losses accumulate indefinitely over time. Take the 1997-98 El Niño: five years on, global losses came to roughly $5.7 trillion, far above the $36 billion estimated at the time. This permanence comes from the fact that the whole world is hit at once, supply chains break in multiple places, and the efficiency of capital allocation falls.

[41:03] (Justin Mankin) **After all this exposure, humans still haven't learned to adapt** — Humanity has been exposed to El Niño for a very long time, and yet the research shows we have not adapted to it effectively. The evidence is that the economic losses remain enormous, which means we have not learned from the feedback. Adaptation strategies include early warning systems, emergency management and insurance products, but coordination at the global level is missing. El Niño can serve as a testing ground for adaptation strategies, providing a reference point for dealing with global warming.

[49:12] (Justin Mankin) **El Niño is a randomized controlled trial run by nature** — El Niño recurs cyclically, but the timing and the intensity of any given event are random, which makes it behave like a randomly assigned treatment. Using that natural experiment, you can compare economic growth in El Niño years against non-El Niño years and identify the causal effect. It is analogous to a randomized controlled trial in medicine: the cycle exists, but the randomness is enough to isolate the effect.

### 术语 / glossary

- Teleconnection (): The physical link between a climate phenomenon such as El Niño and the weather and climate of distant regions.
- RONI / Relative Oceanic Niño Index (): A sea-surface temperature anomaly index built on a rolling baseline, used to measure El Niño intensity.
- Level effect (): A shock that temporarily pushes output away from its level, after which it returns to the original trend.
