## Romans knew the founding myth was false and used it as a diplomatic tool

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-13-ancients-罗马人清楚建城神话是虚构的-但照样当外交工具/
- 节目 / show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Romulus & Remus
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-13 · 时长 / duration: 59:55
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 11269 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Rome's origin myths were not history carved in stone but an elastic narrative Romans used to negotiate, to absorb other peoples, and to digest civil war; the archaeology even contradicts the 753 BC founding date outright.**

为什么听 / why: Rather than arguing over whether Romulus existed, watch how these stories functioned as diplomatic hard currency. The second half, on the archaeological evidence for the break between 753 and 600 BC, adds the most.

### 核心论点 / points

[11:09] (Jeremy Armstrong) **In the early tradition, Aeneas never actually reached Rome** — In Homer, Aeneas is only a minor prince on the Trojan side; when the city falls he carries his father out, and the Greeks let him go out of respect for that piety. He then wanders the Mediterranean, and many cities claimed he had passed through them — but almost no tradition brings him to Rome. Even in Virgil's Aeneid he merely looks over the ground where Rome would stand, finds a community already there, and turns away. His real attachments are Lavinium and Alba Longa; he is linked to Rome only through the bloodline of his descendants. Jeremy stresses that this thread is "very rough, very vague" — nothing like the direct line later Romans claimed.

[17:10] (Jeremy Armstrong) **Rome stitched its foreign policy together with characters everyone knew were invented** — The function of these origin stories was not to record history but to serve as connection points. Because Aeneas wandered so widely, many communities could claim a link to him. By the third century BC, Segesta in Sicily was using Aeneas to get close to Rome: "we are both connected to this man." Jeremy says local elites mostly knew the figure was fiction, but it was "useful and pleasant" — it let them negotiate real political treaties on the strength of it. Greek myth used Odysseus the same way, as a diplomatic go-between for one place after another. Rome's foreign policy, in other words, was stitched together out of characters like this.

[22:33] (Jeremy Armstrong) **The she-wolf nursing the twins predates every written account we have** — The Romulus and Remus story we read today comes mainly from Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all writing centuries after the events. But the core image — twins suckled by a she-wolf — was already standing in the city of Rome around 300 BC, in a statue group dedicated by the Ogulnius brothers, and it appears on early silver coinage. So the story was fixed in elite culture by the end of the fourth century BC at the latest. Jeremy also points out that some details — pastoral raiding, Indo-European mythic motifs — feel archaic, not like something someone in the middle Republic would invent, which implies a long oral tradition behind it.

[32:06] (Jeremy Armstrong) **The she-wolf is not a metaphor for a prostitute — she is a wolf** — "Lupa" means both she-wolf and prostitute, and later writers took it to mean the wife of the shepherd Faustulus. Jeremy's view is the opposite: in the early images it is a wolf, and a wolf that has just given birth is one of the most ferocious animals on the Italian peninsula. Wolves appear throughout the origin stories of Italic peoples such as the Samnites, standing for migration, settlement and ferocity. In choosing the she-wolf, Romans were writing that extreme violence into their own descent. The "prostitute" reading looks more like later Romans humanizing the image in hindsight — he says explicitly that this is only his instinct, not a settled conclusion.

[43:14] (Jeremy Armstrong) **The fratricide encodes Rome absorbing its own Latin kin** — Remus is not just a supporting character in a Roman story; he is a Latin hero in his own right, whose name turns up in other Latin communities, while the name Romulus means, literally, "the Roman." The killing of one brother by the other therefore corresponds to the fourth century BC, when Rome conquered and absorbed the other Latin towns: same stock, yet killed and then integrated. Writing this passage in the first century BC, Livy may also have been using it to answer the trauma of civil war. Jeremy's reading: the story concedes that brother killing brother is terrible, but the point lies in the aftermath — everyone gathers back together into a single community. That is Rome's narrative template for digesting civil war.

[47:15] (Jeremy Armstrong) **Rome grew by abducting and recruiting people, not only by fighting** — After Remus dies, Romulus turns quickly into a cool-headed founder: he finishes the walls, establishes religious rites, and divides the population into 30 curiae, all of which later Romans saw as the germ of their constitution. He also makes Rome an "open asylum" — anyone willing to come may join — but the arrivals are mostly men, and women are lacking. So he schemes to invite the neighbouring Sabines to a festival and has his men carry off the most beautiful women. Jeremy compares an early city to a shopping mall that has to find ways of attracting all kinds of "customers." For Romans, expansion ran on three mechanisms at once — force, intermarriage and attraction — all of them ways of taking outsiders in.

[49:30] (Jeremy Armstrong) **Romans felt no need to settle on one ending for their founder** — Romulus's end is "extremely messy." He disappears while reviewing the army on the Campus Martius and never returns. Two versions dominate: he is wrapped up by lightning and becomes a god, or the senators tear him apart alive — which is hard not to read against Caesar's death. What Jeremy finds most intriguing is that Livy and other writers set the two endings side by side and treat both as acceptable accounts. This founding father can be a god ascending or a tyrant executed by his own people. Romans did not need a single verdict, and that contradiction is exactly what gave later politicians room to take what suited them.

[57:07] (Jeremy Armstrong) **The founding date was reverse-engineered to line up with Greek chronology** — Jeremy cites drilling data from Andrea Brock and others: the Tiber shifted its course around 600 BC, and Rome's geological layout changed with it. That leaves an obvious break between the traditional founding date of 753 BC and the Rome that later served as the city's centre. But he says Romans would not have been troubled by this — in their eyes a city was more a meeting place, an idea and a set of relationships than a physical thing. They used 753 to align with Greek chronology (the first Olympic Games are 776 BC), and anything earlier than that could rest only on "reasonable guesses." The gap between myth and history was not a problem for ancient Romans.

- Casa Romuli (): Post-hole remains on the Palatine that Romans regarded as Romulus's own former hut.

## Elizabeth wanted Mary assassinated, but was forced to sign the death warrant

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-restishistory-玛丽之死背后的真博弈-伊丽莎白想要暗杀-不想签字/

**Elizabeth I did not want Mary executed in public; she hoped someone would kill her privately under the Bond of Association. The Privy Council insisted on legal process, and in the end, even after the Queen had signed, they defied her wishes and rushed the warrant through the night to Fotheringhay.**

为什么听 / why: This episode rewrites Mary's death from a story of religious martyrdom into a judicial murder stage-managed from start to finish by a spymaster, and it lays out what Elizabeth's real options were. Dense with information, though the opening runs long.

### 核心论点 / points

[23:09] (Tom) **What arrived for Mary was not freedom but bait in a beer barrel** — Gifford's scheme used beer deliveries to carry letters: correspondence for Mary went into a waterproof container, the container was pushed through the bunghole of a beer barrel, the barrel was carted to Chartley, and Mary's steward retrieved it. The channel ran both ways, so Mary could write back. But Gifford had already been turned by Walsingham, and the whole ‘French embassy channel’ was watched from behind by Phelippes. Mary believed she was rebuilding contact with the outside world; in fact every letter was opened, read, deciphered and resealed exactly as it had been. What arrived for her was not freedom. It was carefully engineered bait.

[28:50] (Tom) **The decipherer drew a gallows on the transcript to mark evidence, not to predict** — Mary's dictated reply contained the coded reference to the six gentlemen, which was precisely what Phelippes wanted. After deciphering Mary's letter he copied it into English and drew a gallows on the transcript, calling it the ‘bloody letter’. He was not predicting the outcome; he was marking the decisive link in the chain of evidence. Babington and his fellow conspirators were kept in the dark throughout. When Mary was taken out of Chartley on 11 August to hunt deer, she still thought the riders approaching might be her rescuers; in fact it was Walsingham closing the net. Letter, decipherment, gallows: that sequence turned Mary from someone implicated in a plot into the person who had authorized the assassination of a queen.

[38:39] (Tom) **An empty throne exerts more pressure than a queen in the room** — In the presence chamber at Fotheringhay, Elizabeth was not there, but her empty throne sat high beneath a canopy of state, looking down on the whole trial. Lord Burghley took the presiding seat; he had waited decades for this moment. Mary had very little room to maneuver in how she framed her position: she was not an English subject, she was an anointed monarch, and she refused to recognize the court's legitimacy. Burghley sent delegation after delegation to persuade her, and in the end it was Christopher Hatton, with a line to the effect that if she were innocent, avoiding trial would only damage her reputation, who got her to walk in. The moment she entered she found that what faced her was not law but a stage of power whose ending had already been written.

[45:00] (Tom) **Walsingham's answer denied everything and addressed nothing** — In court Mary accused Walsingham of tampering with her letters, which is exactly what had happened. His reply was diplomatic craft of a high order: he swore before God and the world that as a private man he had done nothing unbecoming, and as Secretary of State nothing unworthy of his duty. In principle the sentence denies everything, and yet it answers not one specific charge. Stephen Alford calls it a masterpiece of wording that says everything and nothing at once. Mary then turned to Burghley and said that he truly was her enemy, to which Burghley shot back that he was the enemy of Queen Elizabeth's enemies. By that point the exchange was no longer legal argument. It was a showdown over power.

[53:59] (Tom) **The Puritans refused assassination because justice has to be seen** — Even after signing, Elizabeth did not want the death warrant carried out. What she wanted was for someone, under the oath of the Bond of Association, to privately ‘shorten Mary's life’. Walsingham, though ill, wrote to Mary's keeper Paulet conveying the Queen's displeasure. Paulet's refusal is the crucial moment: he would not make so foul a shipwreck of his conscience, nor leave so great a blot on his posterity, as to shed blood without law and warrant. Elizabeth called him dainty for it. This explains why the Privy Council did not opt for assassination: hardline Puritans though these men were, they believed justice had to be visible, that an execution had to run through legal process and carry God's sanction. Assassination was politically cheap, but in matters of faith it was unacceptable.

[1:03:03] (Tom) **Elizabeth won the law, Mary won the narrative** — Mary removed her black velvet outer garment to reveal a crimson silk petticoat and undergarments, the color of Catholic martyrdom. The Protestants present lost their composure entirely; not one official report mentions this moment, and only the six Catholic waiting women around her spread the detail. The night before, she had written a final letter to Henri III saying she was condemned for her Catholic faith and her claim to the succession, but after her death she was forbidden to declare that she died for Catholicism. The red beneath the black was the visual version of that letter: it turned the execution, in the court of public opinion, into religious persecution. Elizabeth won the law. Mary won the narrative.

[1:05:14] (Tom) **Three strokes, a wig and a dog under the skirts: the execution became farce** — The executioner's first stroke landed on the back of Mary's head, and in agony she cried out for the Lord Jesus to receive her soul; the second stroke reached the neck but still did not sever it, and the executioner had to work the blade like a butcher to part the head from the body. When he lifted the head by custom to display it, all he was holding was a wig, and Mary's head had rolled to the edge of the scaffold. Her women were then led away, and the executioner found under Mary's skirts a Skye terrier she had kept, howling in the pool of blood. These turns made the execution into an excruciating farce, and they also show that Mary played her own script right to the moment of death: what she wanted was not only martyrdom, but to leave her enemies with no dignified way out.

## NVIDIA's VP of Research: The Endgame for Models Is Ecosystem, Not Beating Rivals

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-zhangxiaojun-英伟达研究副总裁-模型竞争终局是生态-不是击败对手/
- 节目 / show: 张小珺·商业访谈录 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/zhangxiaojun/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: 150. 对英伟达研究副总裁刘洺堉的4小时访谈：功夫、Cosmos 3、开源世界模型、黄仁勋、你不需要击败所有对手
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-12 · 时长 / duration: 3:36:12
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 51711 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Ming-Yu Liu: model capabilities will eventually converge, and NVIDIA's open-source world model is not competition but groundwork; physical AI's GPT moment has not arrived, but the conditions are converging.**

为什么听 / why: Ming-Yu Liu is NVIDIA's first, and still rare, case of a researcher promoted all the way to VP. He unpacks the judgment behind how Cosmos was started, converged and open-sourced, and offers a first-hand view of how Jensen Huang manages.

### 核心论点 / points

[4:40] (刘洺堉) **At NVIDIA, world models are a product, not a research project** — Liu gives his title as VP of Research and VP of Cosmos Lab. The team reporting directly to him is roughly eighty or ninety people; adding the other teams inside the company doing Cosmos-related work brings the total to 200 to 300. He is the owner of the entire mission and the person who decides its direction. He stresses that this is a very significant internal program at NVIDIA, and that committing this many people is simply what ‘producing good results’ requires. That headcount is the tell: world models have been elevated inside NVIDIA to a level they have never held before — this is not a research project but an engineering organization with an explicit product mission.

[1:24:21] (刘洺堉) **A manager's recognition has to be aligned with the company's interest** — Liu says he moved up a level every year in his first few years at NVIDIA, and that he may be the first person there to go from researcher to VP. The reason is that he joined early, before the company had AI talent, and helped build NVIDIA's standing in the AI community while explaining internally how AI would affect the business — and at the same time he liked shipping things, which earned trust step by step. Today the team he leads runs up a compute bill of several million dollars a day, and the fact that the company will hand him an operation of that size is what long-term alignment buys. He is emphatic that alignment with the company matters enormously: a pure researcher wants recognition, but a manager's recognition has to be consistent with the company's interest.

[1:41:09] (刘洺堉) **Before Sora, persuading Jensen Huang was hard; after it, easy** — The decision to build Cosmos came around March 2024, right after Sora. Liu says that before Sora appeared, persuading Jensen Huang was fairly hard, and that after Sora it was not hard at all, because Huang saw immediately what it meant for the company. He and a group of researchers working on generative models wrote Huang an email together, asking that NVIDIA build a world model. Huang pulled everyone into a meeting — and told each of them to go away and come up with a product name. Liu's own reaction was that Huang would produce a better name anyway, so why waste the effort; Huang insisted he do it, because the name is bound up with the product's positioning. They settled on Cosmos, and the goal was never creative work: it was to solve problems in the physical world.

[1:54:47] (刘洺堉) **22 models is not richer choice, it is slower iteration** — In the Cosmos 1 era Liu did his own estimate and concluded that covering the range of customer needs might take 22 models. He reported that number in a meeting with Jensen Huang, and Huang answered with Costco: when they cut the number of items on display, sales went up, because too many choices confuse the shopper. Liu also found that he himself could not always tell when to use A and when to use B — never mind an outside user. On top of that, every model has to be maintained, so the more models there are, the slower iteration gets. That is why Cosmos 2 to 3 is such a large gap: a convergence from many models into one unified world model that folds understanding, prediction, generation and action together.

[2:08:22] (刘洺堉) **The dual tower is only a stage; one tower would be enough** — Cosmos 3 uses a dual-tower structure: one tower handles discrete information and is responsible for understanding, the other handles continuous information and is responsible for generation. Liu explains that this is a very sensible choice at the current stage, because keeping discrete reasoning and continuous generation apart means customers doing post-training on one will not disturb the other. If everything were wired together, a customer adjusting the generation distribution could damage the understanding capability. But he says plainly that the next goal is something simpler: ‘why two towers — one tower is enough’. They are moving toward a single tower, while weighing at the same time whether users can get started with it easily; you cannot sacrifice usability in pursuit of engineering perfection. The final architecture is not settled, and will depend on which one has better deployment cost.

[2:31:45] (刘洺堉) **People who fear mistakes stop deciding, so leave room for error** — The Cosmos 3 paper has over 290 authors, just under 300. Liu thinks the core tension in a large team is that you need everyone pointed at the same goal and, simultaneously, every individual able to make decisions on their own. If only a few people decide, progress is slow; if everyone decides for themselves but the goals are not shared, the work diverges or turns into internal horse races. His answer is to put a great deal of thought into how the team collaborates: keep information transparent so everyone has enough of it to make the right call, and provide room to make mistakes, because people who are afraid of being wrong will not make decisions at all. He also stresses that well before the paper existed he had told the main leads exactly what the model would look like, so that everyone could see the same picture — the way a basketball player pictures the ball going cleanly through the net before taking a free throw.

[2:52:41] (刘洺堉) **Not laying people off is slower, but it buys employees who speak up** — Liu says NVIDIA has no forced ranking and does not do layoffs; in his ten years there he has never heard news of a layoff. His view is that employees will only say the things people keep quiet about in places where they fear being cut once they feel safe with the company and trust it; if everyone is scrambling to stand out, cohesion and collaboration get harder. The downside is that when a technology matures, employees need time to learn new things and retrain, which is slower than cutting them and hiring fresh people. What the company gets in exchange is trust and cohesion. Jensen Huang has watched a great many storms pass through Silicon Valley, and choosing this model is a considered decision. NVIDIA runs a marathon, and it does that by positioning early — CUDA, for instance, was a ten-year bet.

[3:07:40] (刘洺堉) **You cannot blame the setup for falling behind; nothing was ever fair** — Liu calls Jensen Huang a ‘hexagonal all-rounder’: he can go down to register-level detail in computer architecture and also talk marketing and pricing, covering every side. He recalls once explaining a gap against a competing product by saying the ‘setting was unfair’, and Huang came straight back with ‘Are you kidding me? Actually, nothing is fair’ — which taught him that doing research means creating the conditions your goal requires, not finding reasons. The core of Huang's management is that Mission is the boss: the company behaves like an organism, and when it decides to move in a direction, the skills of different teams align by themselves. Liu also notes that Huang reads an enormous volume of email every day, hunting for signals and making priority calls, and that this has shaped how Liu now works — switching topics every half hour.

## Bedtime procrastination isn't laziness — it's the self-time your day took away

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-ologies-睡前拖延不是懒-是白天没了自我时间/
- 节目 / show: Ologies (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ologies/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Noctohabitology (SLEEP PROCRASTINATION) with Vanessa “Nessy” Hill
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-12 · 时长 / duration: 1:37:32
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 17170 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 2 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**For most people bedtime procrastination runs only about half an hour; the real problem is a daytime with no autonomy. Blue-light glasses do less than advertised, while indoor lighting matters more. And self-compassion improves sleep more than forcing yourself into bed early.**

为什么听 / why: This episode uses empirical data to strip the guilt out of staying up late, and offers fixes at the level of habit — for anyone who scrolls their phone at bedtime and then beats themselves up about it.

### 核心论点 / points

[5:15] (Alie Ward) **Mainstream sleep advice is something ordinary people simply cannot follow** — After Hill moved from Australia to the United States and went from a steady job to working as a creative, her sleep got worse and she developed short-term insomnia. She found that mainstream sleep advice — no screens before bed, for instance — was very hard for ordinary people to act on, so she went on to do a PhD in behavioral psychology, studying sleep and behavior change. A video she made about sleep deprivation drew 500,000 views, which showed her that sleep science needs a more human way of talking about itself.

[12:43] (Alie Ward) **ADHD may in fact be a disorder of circadian rhythm** — A paper from December 2025 recasts ADHD as a circadian rhythm disorder: close to 80% of patients have a delayed sleep-wake cycle. The treatment suggestions include a fixed wake time, morning light exposure, screen limits, and low-dose melatonin. The key mechanism is that ADHD affects time perception, so people underestimate at night how long a task will take, and push their bedtime back.

[25:54] (Alie Ward) **Refusing to go to bed is how you claw back the self the day took** — Hill's qualitative research found that the core motive behind bedtime procrastination is a fight for "self time": the day is filled up with work and obligations, and only at night does a sense of control return. It shows up most sharply in people starting new jobs, new parents, and caregivers. Night is also a window for exploring identity — LGBTQ+ people, for example, may only be free to express themselves late at night — which makes the procrastination not just avoidance but resistance.

[45:46] (Vanessa Hill) **Most people delay only half an hour, and the internet's story scared them** — The data show that most participants put off bed by 0-30 minutes a night, a smaller group by 60 minutes, and extreme cases by 125 or 175 minutes, or even 2-3 hours. That changed how the researcher defines the problem: many of the people who signed up were not actually delaying for long, but had been frightened by a perfectionist narrative circulating online. The host jokes that she belongs to the extreme group.

[48:50] (Vanessa Hill) **Blue-light glasses are no magic bullet, and misused they make things worse** — Research from 2025 indicates that blue-light glasses are not a magic bullet: the effect depends on the filtering characteristics and on when you wear them, and using them wrong can backfire. The recommendation is to pick a product with an MFD value greater than 1, or to consult Consumer Reports' testing, where the cheap brand Uvex Skyper actually performed best. But the researcher cautions that the crux of sleep-onset procrastination may not be light at all — it may be long-standing habit.

[56:55] (Vanessa Hill) **The main suppressor of melatonin is your room light, not your screen** — Compared with the blue light from devices, indoor lighting suppresses melatonin far more severely. Testing at Monash University found that roughly half of homes have light bright enough to suppress 50% of melatonin. The fix is to switch to warm-colored bulbs, or use smart lights that mimic the flicker of a candle, so the environment naturally "cools down" before bed.

[1:21:58] (Vanessa Hill) **Procrastination is treated with a substitute behavior, not an earlier bedtime** — The lever for changing bedtime procrastination is the habit system: first identify the trigger (time, emotion, place) and the reward you are getting, then hand the slot over to an explicit substitute behavior. For instance, watch one 30-minute episode of a show instead of scrolling endlessly, and set a sleep timer at the same time. The library of behavior change techniques contains 93 methods; the researcher considers monitoring and substitution the most practical.

[1:34:56] (主持人) **Topping up self-time during the day does not dissolve late-night delay** — A 2025 clinical trial tried to dissolve late-night procrastination by topping up "self time" during the day — subjects were encouraged to listen to podcasts or read during their lunch break, their commute, or after dinner. It did not work. The researcher therefore infers that what people need may be precisely the darkness and quiet of night, which a daytime substitute cannot supply. Negative results carry information too, and the scientific community should encourage publishing them.

    译 / zh:

## You don't have to read AI's code line by line, but trust has to be rebuilt

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-pragmatic-ai-写代码不必逐行读-但信任必须重建/
- 节目 / show: The Pragmatic Engineer (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/pragmatic/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Stop being skeptical about AI for development with Charity Majors
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-12 · 时长 / duration: 1:25:32
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 16393 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**AI in 2025 is where the cloud was in 2010. The real question is not whether to read the code AI writes, but when not to read it, and how to rebuild trust with tests, evals, and an honest accounting of the on-call cost.**

为什么听 / why: This episode makes both cases — that AI is turning code into slop, and that AI is an enormous win — and it hands you an operational verification discipline plus an experimental way to deal with the fatigue. Useful whether you want to win the argument or actually ship something.

### 核心论点 / points

[10:13] (Charity) **Whether to read AI-written code is no longer worth arguing about** — Charity says 2025 is to AI what 2010 was to the cloud. At first she treated AI as ‘a feature bigger than a programming language’ rather than a generational shift. The real turn came before Opus 4.5, and what changed was the harness and the tooling, not the model itself. She admits her first round of skepticism was right and her second was wrong. So ‘should you read the code AI writes’ is not worth arguing about anymore; the real questions are when, and under what conditions. Whether that day arrives is no longer the question — the question is when.

[14:16] (Charity) **Once rewriting is cheap, editing in place only accumulates entropy** — Infrastructure has long run on the principle of never fixing a running thing but replacing it, and AI pushes that principle up into application code. When rewriting gets cheap, editing in place accumulates entropy, while replacing resets it to zero. Charity says generating 10,000 variants of a function is faster than hand-writing one, and cost will push the industry toward generate-and-verify rather than manual modification. That is why ‘delete it and start over’ becomes the default move inside AI workflows, and it means an engineer's core skill shifts from writing code to judging and verifying it.

[26:44] (Charity) **If you skip reading every line, you owe that trust back in evals** — If you are not reading the code line by line, you have to rebuild trust with tests and evals. She names conformance testing specifically — confirming that performance boundaries have not drifted. Deterministic systems are not going away; AI has to be domesticated into predictable channels. Her example is HackerRank's ATS: the same resume run 100 times locally scored anywhere between 66 and 99, which shows that ‘AI is not the right tool for every situation’. This is what turns ‘AI is unreliable, so be careful’ from a slogan into a concrete engineering constraint.

[34:11] (Charity) **Never send anyone something you have not read yourself** — The floor is that you do not send people content you have not read. If it takes the recipient longer to read than it took you to generate, it is probably slop. Every send is a claim on someone else's time and attention. AI should be used to think more deeply, not to avoid thinking — though for non-native English speakers and neurodivergent people, using AI can itself be an act of respect. There is no need to invent new standards for quality and respect; the ones we have are sufficient, and the work is to apply them. That gives an operational test for what counts as AI garbage: before you send, ask whether you read it.

[40:23] (Charity Majors) **The AI victory narrative leaves the on-call bill out of the accounting** — Charity mentions that Meta tracks SEV zero internally — its highest incident severity level — and that over roughly the past two months there was a string of them, at Instagram and WhatsApp, the two divisions whose trust and safety and reliability teams had just been removed. She says you cannot deny the connection, though it is only circumstantial evidence. She also credits Intercom for publishing real data: 18 months of declining reliability and code quality, with a possible upturn only recently. Optimists see the wins from rewrites and automated toil; the people carrying the pager only see systems getting worse. Her ask is to tell the whole story and name the costs.

[44:34] (Charity Majors) **AI cutting into software first is an optimistic signal, not bad news** — Why is software AI's killer application? Because software is made of logic and language, and so is AI, which means you can build in guardrails, checks, and validation in a way other fields cannot. She contrasts this with courts going after lawyers who filed hallucinated briefs — no structured data, no way to verify. She also argues that what AI cannot pull off in software probably cannot be pulled off in other industries either, because software has excellent training data in the form of compilable code. That single point flips ‘AI eats the software industry first’ from a pessimistic story into an optimistic one.

[50:44] (Charity Majors) **The central goal of twenty years of DevOps has failed** — The core goal of the DevOps movement for 20 years was to build a feedback loop connecting the people who write code to how that code behaves in production, and that goal failed — the two are still separate fields. Platform teams manage infrastructure, engineers deploy on top of it, and there is no loop. She does think the split is a healthy separation of concerns, though: are you responsible for the stability of the code you deploy, or for the user experience the code creates? Anthropic has a platform team and an Applied AI team internally as well, and the two sides do not see the question of whether engineers will be made obsolete the same way.

[1:19:36] (Charity) **Do not wait for top-down permission; act first, report afterward** — Her answer to AI fatigue is deliberate experimentation: agree as a team not to write AI-generated PR descriptions, or to go without AI on Wednesdays — act first, report afterward. Most leaders will welcome a team that proposes trying something; better still is to run it and then tell your leader what worked, what did not, and what you learned. Do not wait for top-down permission, because leadership does not know what to approve either; only bottom-up action actually wins back control of your time and your calendar. This turns anxiety into a specific move, and it is where the episode lands: inside uncertainty, agency comes from acting.

## A Diabetes Drug That Switches Itself On With Blood Sugar: Live Bacteria Secreting GLP1 on Demand

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-naturepod-活菌当药-让糖尿病治疗随血糖自动开关/
- 节目 / show: Nature Podcast (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/naturepod/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: The probiotic bacteria engineered to treat diabetes
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-12 · 时长 / duration: 19:37
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 3256 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Scientists have engineered E. coli to secrete GLP1 automatically when blood sugar runs high, improving glucose control in mice and in macaques; human trials are still a long way off, but the work opens up the prospect of a living drug that doses on demand.**

为什么听 / why: This episode explains a fundamental mismatch — a fixed-dose drug is both ineffective and risky against blood sugar that keeps moving — and shows the clever molecular brake built to fix it; the eclipse segment comes with a practical guide to watching safely.

### 核心论点 / points

[0:45] **A fixed-dose drug can never keep up with moving blood sugar** — Diabetes is a common disease with a global footprint; the WHO estimates that roughly one in nine people is affected. Existing GLP1 agonists such as Ozempic and Wegovy work well, but there is a fundamental mismatch: the dosing regimen is fixed while blood sugar moves constantly. Overshoot the dose and the side effects are amplified. So the team set out to build a living bacterium that could sense blood sugar and release the therapeutic molecule on demand — a drug that works only when it is needed.

[2:10] **A molecular brake makes the bacteria produce the drug only when glucose is high** — The team engineered E. coli with a regulatory circuit they call a molecular brake. When blood sugar is low, the brake holds GLP1 synthesis in the off state; when blood sugar rises, a signalling molecule is produced inside the bacterium, the brake releases and GLP1 secretion begins; once blood sugar falls back, the signal weakens and the brake goes back on. This closed loop targets the defect in fixed dosing directly, matching the dose delivered to the real-time blood sugar level — dynamic regulation of the kind the body itself performs. The design is nicknamed Gift, for glucose-responsive bacteria.

[3:30] **The live bacteria survive the stomach and still work, in macaques too** — The researchers fed Gift orally to diabetic mice and to macaques. In both animals the bacteria still worked after passing through the stomach and reaching the gut: under high blood sugar the circuit was strongly activated, GLP1 was secreted, and blood sugar control and glucose tolerance improved markedly. On top of that, treated animals showed lower levels of fat accumulation in the liver and less kidney and colon damage than untreated controls, and the mice lost body weight and body fat. GLP1 itself has a weight-loss effect, but these results support the conclusion that delivery by live bacteria is effective, and that it may bring extra benefit to diabetes patients, who are often also overweight.

[5:00] (Ninzi Guan) **This is not one glucose-lowering drug, it is a platform for living medicines** — Guan stresses that the work is still a considerable distance from human trials. The team needs to work out how long the bacteria survive in the body, how long their effect lasts, and how often they would have to be taken by mouth, and it needs to establish long-term safety. But the larger imagination here is the platform: the same sense-and-respond bacterial system could in future be programmed to recognise the signals of other diseases and secrete the corresponding therapeutic molecules, giving rise to a new generation of smart, self-regulating living medicines. That, rather than a single glucose-lowering therapy, is the ultimate goal of the work.

[6:30] **Where mountain lions are present, deer-vehicle collisions drop by 67%** — Combining vehicle-deer collision data with GPS collar and camera trap records, researchers found that the presence of mountain lions — also called cougars or pumas — cuts the probability of a deer-vehicle collision by 67%. Deer actively avoid the forest edges where mountain lions tend to be active, roadsides included, and because mountain lions are night hunters, deer also become less active at night — which is exactly when many collisions happen. The researchers hope that spelling out this unexpected effect will help build public support for coexisting with large carnivores.

[7:42] **A water drop does not just hit rock, it sets the rock ringing** — Past work on erosion by water drops relied mainly on high-speed cameras, which cannot resolve how force is distributed after impact. These researchers switched to surface strain sensors, measuring the deformation of the material beneath a glass plate. They found that in the first 2 milliseconds after a drop lands it generates powerful forces, enough to begin damaging the surface; then, from 2 to 20 milliseconds, the material and the water vibrate together at close to the natural resonant frequency of rock, which may extend microcracks and so accelerate erosion. That offers a new microscopic mechanism for understanding how landscapes evolve.

[10:00] (Lizzie Gibney) **The eclipse sun is dimmer and can still burn through your retina** — During an eclipse the sun is partly covered and the light is weaker, but the harm remains — looking straight at it can cause permanent retinal burns. There are two safe approaches. One is eclipse glasses that meet the ISO standard, whose filters pass only a tiny amount of light, so that with them on you can barely see ordinary objects. The other is indirect projection: use a pinhole camera, a colander, or the gaps between leaves under a tree to project an image of the sun onto the ground. Never look through a telescope or a camera directly unless it is fitted with a professional filter.

[17:00] (Lizzie Gibney) **To study the corona, two satellites build an artificial eclipse in space** — The scientific value of an eclipse is that it lets you observe the corona, which is normally drowned out by the sun's glare. The corona is the sun's outer magnetic atmosphere, reaching temperatures of several million degrees Celsius, far hotter than the roughly 5000 degrees Celsius of the solar surface, and it is the source of solar storms. Space weather can disrupt satellites, power grids and trains, which is why understanding the corona matters so much. The European Space Agency launched the Proba-3 mission specifically for this: two satellites flying one in front of the other create an artificial eclipse so that the corona can be studied continuously. Eclipses seen from the ground remain a rare opportunity.

## AI writing has stalled: long-form nonfiction is the real test of model ability

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-interconnects-ai写作停滞-长文非虚构是模型能力的试金石/
- 节目 / show: Interconnects (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/interconnects/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: I wrote an AI textbook — how long until AI can do it better?
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-12 · 时长 / duration: 12:32
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Official full text · 2452 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- 校验 / verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Models are improving only slowly at long-form nonfiction, which exposes a defect in how they organize knowledge — a more worrying signal than their progress in code and math, because it bears on whether AI can solve open scientific problems.**

为什么听 / why: The author draws on his own experience writing a textbook to show that AI writing has stalled in long form — a warning for anyone counting on AI to run research autonomously, and worth paying attention to.

### 核心论点 / points

[0:00] (Nathaniel) **A model that can't explain settled science won't solve open problems** — Criticism of AI writing clusters around creative writing, on the argument that good writing demands a highly distinctive voice, a point of view, and human depth of expression. But nonfiction writing — filler text, for instance — was one of the things LLMs were genuinely useful for. The author's point is that the stall in long-form nonfiction is an alarming signal for anyone relying on AI to solve open scientific problems on its own. Models struggle to organize and present the most settled science within their own domains, and that ought to be the precondition for solving the open questions.

[1:30] (Nathaniel) **Insight comes from compression, and models are adding entropy instead** — The author argues that current AI progress in science looks more like picking low-hanging fruit and making cross-domain connections than like revolutionary insight. Organizing knowledge is a form of compression, and compression is the necessary condition for insight. In long-form nonfiction, LLMs add entropy instead, and that cannot be stacked indefinitely. Models will depend on humans to steer them. Even so, the author remains optimistic that scientific progress in narrow domains such as mathematics will translate into broader ones.

[2:30] (Nathaniel) **Coding went from mediocre to superhuman; writing has not moved** — The author has just finished a textbook on RLHF, and used LLMs heavily along the way for typesetting, proofreading, and figures. He had expected that publishing a nonfiction book in 2026 would look dated, but the reality is that progress in writing fell far short of what he expected. Some of the models known for their writing, such as GPT-4.5 and Kimi K2, already count as old. Models have gone from mediocre to superhuman at coding and math, yet writing ability has stalled — it feels orthogonal to the other skills.

[3:30] (Nathaniel) **Writing isn't neglected; inference-time scaling hasn't been unlocked for it** — The author's view is that writing has not been neglected — the challenge is simply large and the targeted training data is scarce. There is some low-hanging fruit, such as dedicated toolchains and prompting, but it is unlikely to multiply capability. Writing is a very hard task, and unfortunately we have not yet unlocked inference-time scaling for it. Today's models are bad at long-form technical writing: individual sentences are acceptable, but a whole chapter comes out disorganized and vaguely worded, and it often contains conceptual errors.

[4:30] (Nathaniel) **Models can check every sentence but cannot hold a chapter together** — The author has observed that GPT models are excellent at catching typos and detail-level problems, while Claude models have more taste as editors, grasp the mental model of the task better, and offer interesting suggestions. What these cases show is that models are good at checking the content of each individual unit but bad at stringing the components together, which produces compounding errors. In math and code, RLVR (reinforcement learning from rule-based verification) magically reduced errors of this kind; in writing there is no equivalent yet.

[5:42] (Nathaniel) **Using AI output isn't cheating if an expert vets it, but it's a slope** — The author reports that over the course of writing the book, AI models contributed under 1% of the sentences of technical explanation, because he, as the expert, signed off on those sentences. During editing he used Claude Code to navigate editorial comments, separating simple typos from complex problems and asking for suggestions. His position is that using AI output is not cheating if the expert vets it strictly — but it is a slippery slope, and he did end up accepting some AI suggestions during the full second-draft review.

[7:30] (Nathaniel) **Effort saved in writing costs you the intuition you will need later** — The author stresses that using AI for nonfiction writing erodes the gain in understanding, and that understanding — intuition, taste, instinct — is what will be worth more in the future. If you are not an expert, you cannot spot where the AI is deficient. He wrote the book to give back to the community, so even with AI in the loop, finishing it at all was a win. He grants that more human effort would have meant more learning and a better product, but the deciding factor was the worry that the book would already be dated by the time it was published.

[9:00] (Nathaniel) **The early organizing stage needs insight, and AI is nowhere close** — The author sees AI models as good tools for turning knowledge into other forms, well suited to producing filler material or background content. But the early organizing stage of nonfiction writing requires insight, and there LLMs are nowhere near being a substitute. He would like more experts to use AI to write books, so that more knowledge gets shared; but at present AI saves only 10-20% of the effort, and it will not be the majority any time soon. Social pressure leads some people to conclude that writing a book is pointless, yet high-quality educational content has always been in short supply.

[10:30] (Nathaniel) **Bad prose means the datacenter-genius story does not yet hold** — The author's summary is that models perform excellently in two situations: verifiable domains, and small edits with a lot of context, such as finding a bug or solving a specific math problem. They perform poorly at open-ended prose generation. Long-form writing will be cracked before creative writing, but this is a strong signal that models cannot express the full extent of their knowledge on underspecified problems. That caps their ability to become the "datacenter geniuses" who solve major scientific problems.

## The father of linoleum never trademarked it, and even the name became public property

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-stuffmissed-油毡之父没注册商标-连名字都成了公共财产/
- 节目 / show: Stuff You Missed in History Class (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/stuffmissed/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Frederick Walton and the Invention of Linoleum
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-12 · 时长 / duration: 41:32
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Official transcript · 6831 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Frederick Walton invented linoleum but lost the name because he never registered it as a trademark; the process that actually set the industry standard came from a man on his payroll, C.F. Leak.**

为什么听 / why: Invention history usually gets flattened into a hero story. This episode reconstructs the real commercial system behind linoleum through patents, insurance and an employee's contribution, and founders in materials will find something to take from it.

### 核心论点 / points

[1:01] **He cut off his family fallback before he started experimenting** — Walton was born in 1834 into three generations of cloth frizzers. His father, James, was fiercely secretive about the craft and would not let his son alter the machines. Frederick was fascinated by machinery but did not want to inherit the business, so at 27 he left the family firm for London to work on his own, giving up both his share of the profits and his income from his father's company. This is the starting point for understanding every financial problem that followed: he was not inventing from a position of security, he cut off his retreat first and experimented afterwards.

[5:04] **The paint-skin flash of inspiration was probably tidied up later** — By his own account, a paint can in his laboratory had formed the usual dried film of oil on the surface, and he noticed that this skin held together and had a rubbery elasticity. So he began oxidizing linseed oil systematically, blending in resins and gums to make Campticon, then combining that with coal dust to get a floor cloth similar to Camptulicon. The hosts flag this explicitly: the "he saw the skin on the paint" version may be a neat story constructed after the fact, and the real process was very likely far less smooth.

[10:11] **Early linoleum work was propped up by loans from his father** — Frederick burned through his money fast and proposed that his father advance him his inheritance: a thousand pounds up front, then seven or eight hundred pounds every quarter after that. His father refused and would not even discuss it; the help Frederick got from his brother William was spent too. In the end his father would only lend small sums at interest, Frederick's debts to him ran past eight thousand pounds, and his father cut him off again in anger. This stretch shows that early linoleum development was carried almost entirely on family money, and it explains the attitude he later took to insuring his factory.

[14:19] **Linoleum was not inspiration, it was ground out a few millimeters at a time** — He tried to peel the oxidized oil film off oiled cloth and could not, so he simply ground thin cotton into a pulp, heated rosin, poured the mix onto the floor and let it set; once set, it was cut, aged and milled, then blended a second time with cork dust and pigment. Repeating this cycle over and over built up only a few millimeters in several weeks. To scale it up he built large open oil pans and iron racks, where a single dip of cloth needed about a day to dry. Read this and you see that inventing linoleum was not a flash of insight about "a piece of flooring" but painful process engineering.

[22:28] **Full insurance let him turn a factory fire into an expansion** — His factory at Grove in England burned down a few weeks before his lecture at the Society of Arts. Because the raw materials were highly flammable, Walton had taken out very large, fully covering insurance in advance, so the fire cost him almost nothing financially and he could immediately build a bigger purpose-built plant. In January 1864 he moved again, into a former textile mill at Staines, and in June he founded the Staines Linoleum Manufacturing Company Limited. The genuinely valuable detail here is not the invention but the use of insurance to convert process risk into an opportunity to expand.

[26:39] **What rewrote the industry came from his employee, not from Walton** — Walton's core patent expired in 1877, and competitors began calling their own oil cloth linoleum. He sued and lost, because linoleum had never been registered as a trademark and was ruled a generic name. The bigger turn came in 1880, when his employee C.F. Leak developed a process that used a stencil to drive color all the way through the material to form a mosaic inlaid pattern; Walton kept improving on Leak's foundation and obtained a patent for a continuous inlaid machine in 1890. The process was strong enough that competitors could only buy machines from him. This stretch takes the "lone genius invents it" narrative apart into a corporate system.

[29:42] **Linoleum was once capital-heavy industry, not a cheap substitute** — A late-19th-century German factory was documented in an article titled "Cork Carpets": once the cork dust was milled it went into oil pools that held roughly a million pounds of painter's-grade linseed oil at a time; in the oxidizing rooms the oil turned into long translucent sheets, oxidizing naturally for six to eight months, then was crushed, mixed with fossil resins, kneaded and rolled onto canvas. The author described linoleum as having the warmth and sound absorption of carpet, the elasticity and water resistance of rubber, and the cleanliness of the old oil cloth. It shows that linoleum was once a heavy, large-scale industry rather than a cheap stand-in.

[35:49] **At ninety, the inventor treated religion as a product of evolution** — In 1925 Walton wrote "The Infancy and Development of Linoleum Floor Cloth," and at the end he turned to scientific progress and animal origins. He said he had lived to see everything from railways to airplanes, granted that "our animal origin has undoubtedly been proven," but expressed disappointment that human beings still slaughter one another, holding that it would take millions of years of moral evolution to come close to perfection. He also compared religion to language, arguing both were products of evolution, and sensed that the passage would offend some of his colleagues. The worldview of a ninety-year-old inventor turns out to be more surprising than linoleum itself.

    译 / zh:

## Liberalism Died of the Educated Elite, Not Automation

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-12-tyler-精英化杀死自由主义-自动化并非元凶/
- 节目 / show: Conversations with Tyler (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tyler/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Daron Acemoglu on Liberalism, Automation, and the Educated Elite
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-12 · 时长 / duration: 55:38
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 9782 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Acemoglu dismantles three myths: liberalism is dying of the educated elite rather than automation; AI productivity will not break out for a decade; regulating algorithms is not a restriction on speech, and pro-worker AI is the direction.**

为什么听 / why: A Nobel laureate is pushed by hard counterexamples over the course of the conversation into revising his AI forecast; he lays out the mechanism by which automation lowers the labor share, the difference between an algorithm and the printing press, and what pro-worker AI concretely means. Dense with information, and useful for anyone trying to calibrate their AI narrative.

### 核心论点 / points

[7:53] (Acemoglu) **Conflicts of value cannot be settled by converting everything into utility** — Asked why he does not use utility or cost-benefit analysis to adjudicate conflicts of value, Acemoglu says such methods would themselves require a whole book to specify how everything gets converted into utility and who decides what counts as an externality. He rejects both the absolute priority of a Rousseauian general will and the common denominator of utilitarianism, arguing instead that on individual liberty as the single foundation, one returns to the social level to seek a provisional consensus. Morality, he holds, evolves gradually and under uncertainty, just as science does; it is not a fixed external standard.

[11:35] (Acemoglu) **The problem is not that elites have power but that technocracy is complacent** — Acemoglu traces the crisis of liberalism to two forces: the post-industrial economy has made the educated elite both more powerful and more numerous, while a philosophical turn has assigned them higher priority. He warns that any hierarchy drawn along lines of education, race or income obstructs real freedom; although he himself values expertise, the United States and Europe have developed a complacent technocracy that looks down on ordinary people. What is needed, he stresses, is to avoid that technocracy, not simply to strip elites of power.

[16:05] (Acemoglu) **Automation's first-order effect is to push down the labor share** — Responding to the counterexamples Tyler cites, Acemoglu insists on the micro-level mechanism: automation converts labor tasks into capital, so its first-order effect is to lower the labor share. That does not mean wages or employment must fall, because new tasks can absorb labor, but it is very hard to recover the original share. He cites his own robots paper: blue-collar workers displaced by robots in the 1990s and the 2000s, in jobs such as welding and painting, saw clear wage declines. He objects to treating technology as a black box and argues for distinguishing automation from the creation of new tasks.

[25:00] (Acemoglu) **Even a free-speech absolutist should want algorithmic recommendation regulated** — When Tyler draws an analogy between social media and the printing press spreading Marx and Lenin, Acemoglu replies that human beings have already adapted to carriers like books, but an algorithm can pinpoint Tyler's weaknesses precisely and fan the flames, which is an entirely different world. So he calls himself a free-speech absolutist while supporting regulation of social media's algorithmic recommendation, because he is not restricting what Tyler says, only how the platform exploits Tyler's words. He proposes non-algorithmic timelines, such as showing the accounts you follow in chronological order, as a possible way out.

[29:43] (Acemoglu) **America has already tacitly given up on half its secondary students** — Tyler pushes back on the charge that education has been abandoned by pointing to New York City's high per-student spending. Acemoglu answers that roughly half of American secondary students read and write several grade levels behind, and society as a whole has come to accept this by default. In his view the elite class fills the gap by importing skills rather than being willing to educate its own people, and this is precisely the rupture in the "social contract" he criticizes. He argues for updating that contract so that politicians, journalists and technology leaders genuinely commit to educating Americans, and for restructuring teachers' unions that have become ideological and dysfunctional.

[34:56] (Acemoglu) **AI will not be a game changer within the next ten years** — Acemoglu concedes that if he rewrote his 2023 paper today he would raise his productivity estimate for AI, because models have advanced faster than expected, but progress at the application layer is slow, which drags out adoption. He expects one or two years of rapid growth over the coming decade, with a limited average growth rate: not the game changer McKinsey or OpenAI imagine. On Tyler's proposal of at least half a percentage point of growth, as in the IT period of 1995-1998, he says it will at least be no worse than that, while refusing any utopian or doomsday estimate.

[41:46] (Acemoglu) **Pro-worker AI comes from changing the narrative, not from appointing a regulator** — Asked what regulatory form pro-worker AI would take, Acemoglu explicitly opposes setting up a regulator to decide which kinds of AI are permitted. The pro-worker AI he has in mind lets workers draw on information and tools to do new and complex things, expanding the capabilities of nurses, journalists and engineers. Cultivating it requires changing the narratives and ambitions of technology companies; public policy is only a supporting player. Automation that merely replaces tasks is pro-capital rather than pro-worker, whereas new machines combined with information systems and retraining are the direction to go.

[47:27] (Acemoglu) **Economists use AI to save labor, not to generate new ideas** — On whether AI will raise his own output of papers, Acemoglu says economists at present use it only to save labor; nobody is using it to generate ideas they could not otherwise have had. He grants its value in cleaning data, in meta-analysis, and in turning qualitative historical material into quantitative data, but it has not yet delivered a breakthrough. He offers the Beatles and Beethoven as examples that quantity and quality often go together, so writing more papers raises the probability of top-tier output, but as things stand AI has not changed how he innovates.

## Behind a 0.33Å Error: Drug Design Is Moving From Waterfall to Agile Loop

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-11-latentspace-0-33å-误差背后的信号-药物发现正转向敏捷闭环/
- 节目 / show: Latent Space (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/latentspace/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: 🔬The BioAI Phase Shift - Matthew McPartlon & Neil Patil, Chai Discovery
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-11 · 时长 / duration: 1:35:19
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 20603 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Chai designed antibodies for 50 targets and got hits on about half of them, with cryo-EM validation showing a 0.33Å error. The real moat is not the model — it is data, compute, and a validation pipeline pharma companies will actually pay for.**

为什么听 / why: Dense throughout, and the back half is where the value is: compute allocation, the conflict between architectural complexity and the bitter lesson, and the economics of GLP-1 all come with specific numbers and specific judgments. Worth a second listen for founders and engineers.

### 核心论点 / points

[0:00] **Drug discovery should run as an agile loop, not a waterfall** — The analogy for biological design is software tooling: an interface closer to a design suite like Photoshop, where a tool in the spirit of ‘content-aware fill’ has Chai generate a binder for you. Traditional drug discovery is a waterfall — target discovery, hit discovery, then optimization, strictly in series, with each gate taking months to years, which makes early-stage trial and error extremely expensive. If a model can reliably hand you promising candidates, that sequence turns into a loop, much the way software development moved to agile. The next rung of abstraction to climb is agonists, ADCs, and precisely triggering switches inside cells.

[7:27] **Hit rates only rose after switching to CRO-validated targets** — Chai ran an internal challenge: design antibodies against 50 targets. The first pass picked targets that were ‘interesting’, and half of them did not work. The team then switched to targets a CRO had already validated, choosing from the CRO's own catalog. In the end, roughly half of the 50 targets produced hits, with an average binding hit rate of about 20%. This is the experiment that got pharma companies to believe there was a real signal here, and it explains why the large pharma companies were willing to sign big deals.

[18:54] **Open-sourcing Chai 1 was a forcing function for building infrastructure** — Chai 1 does structure prediction, it was open sourced, and the team behind it was five people. The point of building Chai 1 was not the model itself — it was using the model as an excuse to build the infrastructure, MSA and everything around it, properly and in one pass, as a forcing function for a long-term investment. Both co-founders have ties to OpenAI, OpenAI led the seed round, and for a stretch the team sat in OpenAI's office. In the 48 hours before release they pulled all-nighters standing up the web server, and Josh went on Bloomberg TV at 7am with not a single employee in the office.

[34:15] **The 0.33Å figure is not data leakage but atomic-level accuracy** — In the Chai 2 paper, the predicted structure was overlaid on the cryo-EM electron density and you cannot see the difference: the error is 0.33Å, one third the width of an atom. The team's first assumption was that the other side had simply mailed back their own design, or that there was data leakage somewhere. But they had deliberately chosen targets with no known antibody binder, so this was the first antibody hit against that target. This validation is direct evidence that structure prediction has reached atomic-level accuracy.

[52:08] **Antibodies have no evolutionary template, so MSA stops working** — An epitope is the site on a protein you want to block, and identifying it is harder than finding an antibody, because it requires global understanding. Even the multimer version of AlphaFold2 is correct on only about 11% of antibody-antigen binding predictions — meaning 90% are wrong. The crux is MSA. An MSA functions as a structural template, and antibodies are precisely the case where evolution cannot supply a template: every person has to generate unique antibodies against the antigens they personally have encountered, relying on recombination to match pathogens that have never been seen.

[1:02:33] **Compute is power-law distributed and startups fight over the leftovers** — Starting last September, spot and on-demand compute went short again and again, forcing Chai to stockpile its own cards. Compute is power-law distributed: of ten thousand B300s shipped, say, the hyperscalers and the top AI labs take 95%+, and startups fight over the remainder. On top of that, the new hardware is built for LLMs — large KV caches, 72-chip interconnects — so this class of structure model needs its own inference optimization. Technically, the batched attention in Chai-1 has L³ complexity, memory bandwidth binds harder than flops, and even layer norm can turn out to be expensive.

[1:09:02] **Complexity fights the bitter lesson, and the right move is subtraction** — Complexity and the ‘bitter lesson’ principle are in fundamental conflict. AlphaFold 3 may have 23 submodules — the speaker says he is not certain of the count — and a system like that is extremely hard to optimize and to do research on: change one submodule and it moves everything else. The reflexive idea is to add another module, but perhaps the right move is subtraction. Chai's engineering culture leans hard toward simplicity, and a comparison of SpaceX's Raptor 1 and Raptor 2 engines hangs on the office wall as a reminder to keep deleting things. Part of why AlphaFold 2 and 3 succeeded is that they are relatively small models — compute-intensive and data-efficient.

[1:24:23] **GLP-1 brings in more revenue than every AI lab combined** — Measured per token, pharma may be the field with the highest downstream value per token: a single drug can be a multi-billion-dollar asset, and the two classes of GLP-1 drugs together may add up to a trillion-dollar asset. By Chai's estimate, up until three months ago GLP-1's total revenue exceeded that of all AI labs put together, while its market capitalization is relatively far lower. Pharma is fundamentally a VC-style business — one of the largest early venture returns in Silicon Valley was Genentech in the 1980s — and the biggest problem in all of biopharma is precisely its funding model.

### 术语 / glossary

- binder (): A candidate molecule that binds to a target; in this episode, an antibody or antibody fragment.

- durable execution (): An engineering pattern that lets long multi-step processes retry automatically and resume from where they stopped.
- bitter lesson (): The principle in AI of substituting compute and search for hand-encoded domain knowledge.

## A 4x-Levered Bet on the AI Narrative: How a Genius Fund Died of Volatility Drag

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-11-patrickboyle-天才叙事败给波动率拖累-纸上英雄到破产只需一场婚礼/
- 节目 / show: Patrick Boyle (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/patrickboyle/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: Does Leopold Have Situational Awareness?
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-11 · 时长 / duration: 39:37
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 5870 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Aschenbrenner's failure was not a failure of intelligence. It was what happens when you put 3-4x leverage behind a single high-volatility AI theme: volatility drag and asymmetric payoffs made losing control a matter of arithmetic. Markets do not reward concentrated, narrative-driven bets.**

为什么听 / why: This episode takes apart the mathematical inevitability of a highly levered, one-directional, concentrated bet, with the gap between how Silicon Valley and Wall Street think running all the way through it. It is useful because it redefines ‘failure’ — not luck, but arithmetic.

### 核心论点 / points

[4:28] (Patrick Boyle) **You can get the expected value right and still be ruined by repeated bets** — Aschenbrenner is a believer in effective altruism, a school of thought that encourages taking risks with high expected returns even when repeating the wager leads to certain ruin. That is the seed of everything he did later: correct in theory, fatal in practice. The show connects that philosophy directly to how FTX ended — you think you are managing risk, when in fact you are just talking yourself into ignoring the tail.

[8:51] (Patrick Boyle) **The 165-page AI prophecy was a Silicon Valley group chat, written down** — Boyle read every page of ‘Situational Awareness’ and concluded it is not prophecy but a roundup of views the San Francisco crowd had already talked to death. The essay contradicts itself — professing faith in the private sector on one page while calling for the government to nationalize the AI labs on another. Its popularity came not from insight but from restating the industry group chat back to readers in a form that made them feel they had a grip on the future.

[11:13] (Patrick Boyle) **One PDF underwrote a $45 billion trading book** — Aschenbrenner had no prior trading experience. He claims he shorted the market in 2020, but he was 17 at the time and could not have opened a brokerage account. On the strength of a 165-page PDF and some podcast appearances, he raised $225 million from Silicon Valley, and after leverage the trading book reached $45 billion — all of it run by 8 employees. This is not a question of competence. It is structural absurdity.

[14:22] (Patrick Boyle) **New York passing on the deal, unanimously, was the smartest decision that night** — Silicon Valley asks: can it be built? Washington asks: whose permission do we need? Wall Street asks: what if we're wrong? Aschenbrenner's essay converted into enormous checks in Silicon Valley, but New York institutional investors asked the standard question: what happens if the AI revolution doesn't arrive on schedule? His answer was ‘I genuinely believe it will happen’. No detailed plan, no contingency for the position. The New York money passed, unanimously — in hindsight, the smartest risk decision of the night.

[16:29] (Patrick Boyle) **Both the longs and the shorts were bets on the same AI story** — The logic of a traditional long/short fund is to buy the good companies and short the bad ones, stripping out broad market risk and keeping only stock-selection skill. Aschenbrenner bought chip stocks and shorted software stocks — both sides of the book betting on the same AI story. The moment the market doubted that AI would make money soon, the longs fell and the shorts rose, and he lost on both sides at once. In Matt Levine's words: this did not reduce risk, it concentrated risk in a different direction.

[22:52] (Patrick Boyle) **After losing $30 billion, he called it a rare opportunity** — In the letter he sent investors after the losses, he described the market turmoil as ‘ructions’ — Boyle's dig is that the word suits a neighbor failing to pick up after their dog, not losing $30 billion during your own wedding. But the letter is the real highlight: he called this a rare opportunity and invited investors to add to their positions on August 1, while he took one-on-one calls with furious investors from his honeymoon.

[26:03] (Patrick Boyle) **Citadel taking the book was not a rescue, it was an auction** — Citadel bought the entire collapsing portfolio, but this was not a rescue, it was an auction. Griffin beat out Jane Street and Millennium to win the bid. Jane Street was itself an investor in Aschenbrenner's fund, coming full circle to bid for his wreckage. The same thing happened with Enron, Amaranth and SoCo — Griffin is always the first to smell smoke, and he is the last person you want to see when you are the one on fire.

[31:21] (Patrick Boyle) **At 4x leverage, even a great expected return compounds to zero** — This is the mechanism that killed the fund: leverage scales returns linearly, but volatility drags on compounding as a square. Suppose the AI stocks you hold have an expected return of 15% a year with 40% volatility; unlevered, you compound at 7%. Lever 4x and the expected return becomes 60%, but volatility drag goes from 8% to 128%, pulling you back to negative 68% growth. The expected value looks fine; the path goes to zero with certainty.

### 术语 / glossary

- volatility drag (): The compounding loss caused by high volatility: the realized growth rate is roughly the mean minus half the variance.
- margin call (): The broker's forced demand that a fund immediately post more cash or liquidate positions when collateral value falls short.
- expected return (): The probability-weighted average of all possible returns; easily inflated by extreme good outcomes on the right tail, which masks the real risk of a losing median.
- long/short equity (): Holding longs and shorts simultaneously to hedge out broad market moves while retaining stock-selection skill — but if both sides bet on the same theme, the hedge is meaningless.
- lockup agreement (): The contractual term by which a fund bars redemptions for a set period, restricting investors from pulling money out during a crisis.
- full Kelly (): Betting a single position up to full leverage in pursuit of maximum logarithmic growth, ignoring volatility and the risk of permanent loss. Cliff Asness used it to needle the fund's approach.
