## Rammed by Her Own Fleet: The 1%-Cost Torpedo Boat That Created the Destroyer

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-10-historyhit-鱼雷艇用1-的战列舰成本-逼出了驱逐舰兵种/
- 节目 / show: History Hit (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/historyhit/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: The Naval Revolution: Triumph and Disaster
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-10 · 时长 / duration: 36:58
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 6664 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In 1908 a 380-ton destroyer was rammed and sunk by a 10,000-ton cruiser during an exercise, killing 35 men. Behind the tragedy sits the torpedo boat, which overturned naval warfare at about 1% of a battleship's cost and forced the destroyer into existence.**

为什么听 / why: The analogy ‘torpedo boat = today's drone’ is worth the hour on its own; the engine telegraph found in the wreck and the still-unexplained turn make the military-history detail unusually concrete.

### 核心论点 / points

[8:33] **The price of one torpedo boat was enough to sink a battleship** — The arrival of the torpedo worried the Royal Navy badly: you no longer needed another battleship in order to sink a battleship. The episode uses today's drones as the analogy for this kind of asymmetric threat — a torpedo boat cost only about 1% of a battleship's price, yet it could close on a capital ship under cover of darkness and fire. That was a change in the rules of naval combat: until then, sinking a battleship meant big guns trading fire with big guns; now a small platform could do it. Which is precisely why Britain had to find a new counter, on both cost and numbers.

[11:06] **The destroyer is a ship type the torpedo boat forced into existence** — To chase down and intercept torpedo boats, the Royal Navy put the problem out to the shipyards in the 1890s: build a fast ship that could make 30 knots and you were in the fleet. Tiger was a product of that new type, driven by 4 Normand boilers giving about 6,400 shaft horsepower, carrying 86 tons of coal, her volume stuffed with weapons and machinery. The type was first called the torpedo boat destroyer, later shortened to destroyer, and it became the backbone of the twentieth-century fleet — escort, anti-submarine work, air defence — with today's guided-missile destroyers all descended from it.

[14:20] **The faster a ship ran on trials, the sooner she broke down later** — Tiger carried only 57-58 men in total, with minimal living space, and was known as a very wet ship: hot, vibrating, pitching badly in heavy weather, with poor seakeeping. The bridge was completely open, with no radar, no GPS and no radio; at night there was nothing to navigate by but compass and dead reckoning. Crueller still, engineers at the time had an in-house joke: the faster a ship ran on her speed trials, the more prone to breakdown she was afterwards, because running at full speed did structural damage to the hull. This is what it looked like when a navy pushed both men and machinery to the limit.

[19:09] **The 1908 night exercise was preparation for Germany** — The April 1908 exercise was not a display. An ‘attacking force’ of more than ten destroyers set out from Portsmouth and worked through their own fleet in the dark, simulating torpedo launches with flashing signals to prove they could get in close without being detected. It was run with every ship darkened and no moonlight, because there was no radar and no radio then and reconnaissance was done entirely by eye; destroyers could also deploy quickly along the coast and take on intelligence gathering. Training of this kind was seen as necessary preparation for a war drawing closer — the German fleet was already strong enough.

[23:15] (Dave) **Nobody knows why she turned to port that night** — On the night of the accident Tiger was under orders to follow the leading ship, HMS Recruit, but in the darkness all that was visible was the wake ahead. No one has ever explained why she suddenly turned to port, cutting across Berwick's course. Dave's personal judgement is that they simply never saw Berwick — had they seen her, they would not have crossed in front of a giant ship bearing down on them. That night there were many formations of large ships, dense manoeuvring and total darkness; the accident was almost unavoidable. Years earlier, Tiger had already come close to a collision in a similar exercise.

[25:00] **A ram designed to kill enemies cut open a friendly ship** — Berwick displaced about 10,000 tons; Tiger displaced 380 tons light and 425 tons at full load — a difference in mass of 20-25 times. The irony goes further: what Berwick carried in her bow was a ram, designed specifically to sink enemy ships, a ‘weapon of the future’ — and in a peacetime exercise it cut into a friendly ship like a hot knife through butter. By the time the two saw each other there were only about 100 yards left; in a few seconds there was no time at all to react. Berwick's bow made the tragedy unavoidable, however unintended.

[27:38] **She went down in three minutes and no one on the bridge survived** — The collision happened at 8:15 pm; within 3 minutes the stern was under water, and 1-2 minutes after that the bow disappeared. Of the 57-58 crew, 35 died in the lower compartments, including the captain, Lieutenant William Middleton. No one on the bridge survived, so who gave the orders in those last few seconds, and why, will never be known; the court martial could not explain it either. The tragedy was major national news at the time: King Edward VII sent a personal message of condolence, questions were asked in Parliament, and the navy sent several cruisers and tugs to search for days — without ever finding the wreck.

[31:24] **The engine telegraph pointer still stands at ‘full ahead’** — The dive team found Tiger at 62 metres off the Isle of Wight; because they were using specialist rebreathers, their time underwater was limited. The first thing Leo saw was the fourth Normand boiler aft, which immediately confirmed this was a 30-knotter. The most important evidence came from the engine telegraph: the pointer still stands at ‘full ahead’, and the rudder indicator shows only 5-7 degrees of starboard helm, meaning she had neither slowed down nor made any pronounced turn. Yet the transmission chain from the bridge to the engine room was severed at the moment of impact, so even an order given could not have got through. The wreck is well preserved: compass, wheel, telegraph and ship's bell are all still in place.

## Philip Sidney died of a leg wound and became famous at his funeral

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-09-restishistory-philip-sidney-之死-英雄是被葬礼制造出来的/
- 节目 / show: The Rest Is History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/restishistory/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: 695. Elizabeth I vs The Catholics: The Shadow War (Part 5)
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-09 · 时长 / duration: 1:01:55
- 文稿来源 / transcript: Machine transcription · 10532 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 7 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**The Anglo-Spanish cold war turns hot, and Philip Sidney finally gets his chance at glory on the battlefields of the Low Countries — only to die of a leg wound that need not have killed him. What made him a hero of Protestant Europe was the funeral, not the fighting.**

为什么听 / why: The episode uses Sidney's personal fate as the thread through the 1585 turning point in the Anglo-Spanish conflict, and it is clear on court politics, economic warfare and the siege of Antwerp. The drawback is that the information density is not especially high, and the substance is concentrated in the middle and later stretches.

### 核心论点 / points

[6:11] **The courtier the Queen trusted least was the perfect courtier** — At the 1581 tilt, Philip Sidney was the star of the show: born into England's top-tier network of connections, and a poet and courtier famous across Europe, with ‘Astrophil and Stella’ regarded as the sonnet sequence second only to Shakespeare's. But Elizabeth did not really trust him. She resented that his connections were too strong, that he was too independent, too militantly Protestant; keeping him at court to entertain the French marriage embassy looked more like a humiliation. In a quarrel on the tennis court that same year, the Earl of Oxford called him a puppy, and the Queen personally rebuked him for forgetting the difference in rank. He was not knighted until 1583, at 29 — and for a ‘perfect courtier’ like this, the lateness was itself a mark of coldness.

[15:00] **The border between the Netherlands and Belgium was drawn by this war** — Around 1585, Parma had already recovered most of the southern Low Countries for Spanish control; Ghent fell, then Brussels, and the rebel camp looked as though it was about to collapse. Four great rivers formed a natural dividing line: the northern provinces held Spain off in the end and became the Dutch Republic of seventeenth-century Protestantism, capitalism and Rembrandt; the south returned to the Habsburgs and Catholicism, and two and a half centuries later became Belgium. This shadow war between England and Spain also, along the way, decided where the borders of the Low Countries sit on the map of Europe today.

[22:09] **Drake and Sidney were both waiting for the war they knew was coming** — Back from his circumnavigation, Drake bought four mansions, sat as an MP, served as mayor of Plymouth, and even legislated to regulate the cod trade — and was bored out of his mind. Sidney served from 1583 as Master of the Ordnance, responsible for England's defensive preparations. Both were like Churchill in the 1930s, convinced that a war to the death with Spain was closing in, and both held to a militant Protestantism. Their mutual admiration was no accident: one wanted a real war, the other wanted a fellow traveller. By 1585 the war had actually arrived.

[26:45] **Orange's death very nearly brought the Dutch revolt down with him** — On 10 July 1584, William of Orange was assassinated in Delft, crying out as he died ‘God have mercy on me and on my poor people’. He was the symbol of the Dutch revolt and its spiritual and military leader; with his death the rebels nearly collapsed. Facing them was the most formidable general in Europe, Parma — governor of the Netherlands and commander of the army at once, able to do diplomacy and able to fight. When he took over in 1578 the Spanish army was close to collapse; by 1584 he had taken back almost the entire south. France, meanwhile, was paralysed by the War of the Three Henrys, and Philip II finally had his hands free.

[32:13] **Antwerp did not fall to an army, it fell to a bridge** — Antwerp was the largest, richest and most strongly Protestant city in the Low Countries. Parma laid siege from June 1584, and the heart of the operation was building a pontoon bridge nearly half a mile long to cut the Scheldt. The Dutch floated fireships packed with explosives down at the bridge; one did blow out a section and killed 800 Spanish soldiers, but Parma repaired the bridge before the gap could be exploited. In May the rebels attacked again, and the tide carried their own fireships back into their own lines. The siege lasted 13 months; Antwerp fell on 17 August 1585, and more than half of its inhabitants left.

[41:51] **Elizabeth sent troops for trade, not for the Protestant cause** — Three days after Antwerp fell, Elizabeth signed the Treaty of Nonsuch with the Dutch rebels, sending 6,350 infantry and 1,000 cavalry and, unusually for her, agreeing to subsidise the costs. This was not a sudden appetite for war: Philip II had already imposed an embargo on English shipping in May 1585, and if Antwerp passed into Spanish hands the whole trading artery of the Low Countries could be squeezed shut. She demanded three ports as cautionary towns, to be garrisoned by English troops, to make sure she could control the mouth of the Scheldt. Sensitivity about money moved this queen more than enthusiasm for the Protestant cause.

[46:07] **Wrecking your enemy's credit is deadlier than seizing his silver** — Sidney was originally to sail with Drake's fleet to the West Indies, but the Queen recalled him and sent him to Flushing instead. Drake stormed Vigo, San Domingo and Cartagena in turn, dismantling cities to extort ransoms; he intercepted no treasure ship, but he exposed the fragility of Spain's American empire to the financial world of Europe. The Pope and the dukes of Florence and Savoy refused to lend Philip II any more money, and a bank in Seville failed. Burghley remarked with satisfaction that Drake was the man the King of Spain feared most. The genuinely valuable idea in this episode is that strategists in the sixteenth century already understood that attacking an opponent's credit is more lethal than robbing him of gold and silver.

[54:14] **Sidney's standing as a hero was manufactured by his funeral** — Sidney charged three times at the battle of Zutphen; as he turned on the third, a shot hit him above the left knee and shattered the bone. Surgery to extract the bullet brought on gangrene, and he died on 17 October, aged only 31. At the end he sighed over a life of ‘vanity of vanities’. What actually turned him into a hero was the funeral: the coffin carried from Arnhem to London, fourteen pallbearers at St Paul's, the Lord Mayor in attendance, 300 armed Londoners, and his warhorse dragging a broken lance. In death he received the adoration of all Protestant Europe that he had sought in vain while alive. The myth of the hero was made at the funeral.

## Subsea Fiber Is Becoming the World's Largest Listening Network: Not Spycraft, Physics

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-09-asianometry-暗光纤正在把海底变成全球最大窃听网/
- 节目 / show: Asianometry (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/asianometry/)
- 原集标题 / original episode: The Dark Fiber Listening Network
- 发布 / published: 2026-08-09 · 时长 / duration: 20:29
- 文稿来源 / transcript: YouTube captions · 2943 words · timestamps are exact
- 校验 / verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) turns ordinary fiber-optic cable into a continuous vibration monitor. Oil and gas well surveys, earthquake monitoring, whale tracking and anti-submarine ship detection all run on the same technology chain, and the ocean is rapidly losing its privacy.**

为什么听 / why: Dense with numbers, and it follows the full arc of the technology's evolution in one clean line, from the wellbore to the whale to the submarine. But it only covers what the technology can do; it never works through the commercial arithmetic or the economics, so do not expect investment analysis.

### 核心论点 / points

[3:10] **The scattering that makes the sky blue is also the source of the eavesdropping** — Attenuation in optical fiber comes mainly from scattering. Brillouin scattering is produced by low-frequency phonons, which temperature or strain can induce; Raman scattering comes from molecular vibration and is commonly used for temperature measurement. But the most significant of the three is Rayleigh scattering, where light is reflected back by density fluctuations smaller than its own wavelength. Those fluctuations act like tiny mirrors scattered along the entire length of the fiber, sending a small fraction of the light back the way it came. Rayleigh scattering transfers no energy and does not change the frequency of the light. It is the reason the sky is blue, and it is the source of every signal DAS uses: both OTDR and, later, DAS are picking up this reflected light.

[5:22] **Polarization sensing failed because too many causes produce the same change** — In the 1980s, OTDR was commonly used to locate breaks in a cable: send a pulse of light, measure the arrival time of the Rayleigh backscatter, and pinpoint the break or the high-loss section. In 1981, AJ Rogers at the UK's Central Electricity Research Laboratories proposed polarization optical time domain reflectometry, hoping to work backward from changes in polarization to external factors such as temperature, strain and sound. In the 1980s that path failed: too many things change polarization, so a given change could not be attributed to a single cause. The Rayleigh signal is the sum of all the fluctuations along the whole fiber, so the signal is over-averaged, and temperature sensing did not work either. The industry turned instead to Raman and Brillouin scattering: weaker signals, but ones whose Stokes and anti-Stokes frequency shifts map deterministically onto temperature and acoustic strain.

[7:25] **The navy did not commercialize DAS; oil wells did** — Three breakthroughs turned Rayleigh backscatter from a diagnostic tool into a sensing method: lasers with narrower linewidths, meaning purer light; computing power able to sample tens of thousands of times per second; and a clear commercial demand. The US Navy did some early work here, and it remains semi-classified to this day. What actually broke DAS through into commercial use was the oil and gas industry: in the mid-1990s, oil companies began using fiber to monitor wellbores. Downhole temperatures run around 200°C and pressures reach up to 2,000 bar, a harsh enough environment to wear out any electronics; the fiber approach puts all the sensitive equipment on the surface, leaving nothing but cable down the hole.

[11:38] **Fiber VSP won on speed, not on accuracy** — The oil and gas industry first used Raman scattering and the anti-Stokes signal for distributed temperature sensing (DTS), then in the late 2000s applied Rayleigh-scattering DAS to vertical seismic profiling (VSP). Conventional VSP relies on an array of geophones lowered into the well, roughly seven of them strung together per run, with the whole array repositioned after each measurement, which is slow and expensive. The fiber approach has a slightly lower signal-to-noise ratio than wireline geophones, but it is already close, and the killer application is speed: in some cases it finishes in minutes where the geophone approach takes 10 hours. The early challenge was data processing, since DAS can generate up to 10,000 times as much data per second as an ordinary temperature sensor.

[12:38] **Seismic stations are too expensive to deploy; dark fiber is already in the ground** — Teams at Berkeley and Stanford applied DAS to earthquake monitoring in the early 2010s. Conventional seismic stations are costly, which rules out deploying them in bulk; meanwhile telecom and technology companies have laid vast amounts of unused dark fiber, which Berkeley Lab's Ajo-Franklin estimates at roughly 1 million kilometers worldwide, growing by another 100,000 to 200,000 kilometers a year. These cables float freely underground rather than being anchored in place, and earthquakes are extremely low-frequency signals, so picking them out of the noise of cars and trains is hard. Even so, the teams successfully tracked hundreds of small earthquakes both on campus and in the field, some with epicenters as far away as Mexico.

[15:46] **One cable already on the seafloor is worth ten thousand seismometers** — Seismic monitoring networks are even scarcer on the ocean floor than on land. Giuseppe Marra's team at the UK's National Physical Laboratory used laser interferometry, which is related to DAS but not quite the same thing, to detect a major earthquake in central Italy from within the UK, and did it with a cable that had not been laid for earthquake monitoring. The Berkeley team went further: Nate Lindsey used a four-day maintenance window on a subsea fiber cable in Monterey Bay to turn 20 kilometers of cable into 10,000 sensors, recording a small earthquake and also revealing multiple fault zones on the seafloor. A four-day window, an existing cable, ten thousand listening points: that is the paradigm that turns dark fiber into an asset.

[16:50] **It can hear elephants on the railway tracks, and it can hear whale song** — The applications quickly outgrew earthquakes. Back in 1993, Taylor and Lee at Texas A&M filed a patent for intrusion detection based on Rayleigh backscatter, covering large-perimeter protection scenarios such as airports and high-speed rail. Indian Railways even uses it to detect elephants walking onto the tracks. The most striking use is marine biology: by 2022, DAS could track the songs of baleen whales in the open ocean using existing subsea cables. The undersea acoustic environment is noisier than land, with internal waves, sediment transport and storms, but with grid search and Bayesian filtering, tracking is now close to automated.

[18:55] **A ship can switch off its transponder, but not its acoustic signature** — In 2021, Diane Rivet's team in France found that DAS could track an oil tanker at a depth of 2,000 meters, that it worked best in 85 meters of shallow water, and that it could hear a tanker's engine and equipment noise from 2 kilometers away. Conventional passive sonar arrays, civilian or military, are reported to cost anywhere from hundreds of millions to billions of dollars; DAS covers a wider area using cable that is already there, and it will only get stronger as computing power and AI recognition improve. A ship can switch off its transponder to evade satellites, but it cannot switch off its acoustic signature, and threats like an anchor dragging along the seabed can also be flagged in advance. The host's conclusion: perhaps before long, the ocean will be less private than it has ever been.

### 术语 / glossary

- DAS (Distributed Acoustic Sensing) (): Uses the way the Rayleigh backscatter signal in an optical fiber changes with external vibration and strain to turn an entire cable into a continuously distributed vibration sensor.
- Dark Fiber (): Fiber that has been laid but carries no traffic, mostly pre-installed by telecom companies as spare capacity, and available for temporary use as DAS.
- OTDR (Optical Time Domain Reflectometry) (): A diagnostic tool that sends pulses into a fiber and analyzes the arrival time of the backscattered return to locate breaks or high-loss points.
- VSP (Vertical Seismic Profiling) (): A technique that fires acoustic waves into the ground and receives the reflected signals inside the well, used to image the rock around a reservoir.
- Geophone (): The electronic vibration sensor lowered into a well in conventional seismic surveying: expensive, fragile, and limited to discrete measurement points.
- Rayleigh Scattering (): The scattering of light by particles or density fluctuations smaller than its wavelength; the reason the sky is blue, and the source of the DAS signal.

谁该听 / who: Investors in subsea cable and ocean-sensing plays, engineers working on earthquake monitoring or underwater target identification, and policy researchers who care about maritime security.
可跳过 / skip: The first 4 minutes on fiber physics and the taxonomy of scattering can be skipped. Everything from the oil and gas VSP section onward (roughly 7:25) is the good part.
